column1: Three things English speakers should be most careful about: tell apart plain, strong and tight sounds (ㄱ ㅋ ㄲ), do not add a vowel after a final consonant, and do not say ㅓ and ㅗ (or ㅡ and ㅜ) the same.
column2: 说中文的人最需要注意的三点：区分平音、送气音和紧音 (ㄱ ㅋ ㄲ)；不要在韵尾后面加元音；不要把 ㅓ 和 ㅗ (或 ㅡ 和 ㅜ) 发成一样。

column1: Almost every place where spelling and sound differ can be explained by four rules: linking, nasal sounds, tense sounds, and strong (aspirated) sounds.
column2: 拼写和发音不同的地方，几乎都可以用四条规则来解释：连音、鼻音化、紧音化和送气音化。

column1: There is a lot of grass.
I stick the documents with glue.
The water is not coming out.
I gained weight after coming to Korea.
Did you turn off the light?
Yes, I closed the door too.
Used to say "… is …". It is like "am/is/are" in English, but it comes at the end of the sentence.
column2: 用来表示 "……是……"。相当于中文的 "是"，但放在句末。

column1: With a final consonant use "이에요"; without one use "예요".
After a noun with a final consonant (받침), add "이에요". After a noun without a final consonant, add "예요".
column2: 在有韵尾 (받침) 的名词后加 "이에요"，在没有韵尾的名词后加 "예요"。

column1: In English, "am/is" comes in the middle (I am a student), but in Korean it comes at the end (저는 학생이에요).
column2: 中文的 "是" 放在句子中间 (我是学生)，而韩语放在句末 (저는 학생이에요)。

column1: If you raise your voice at the end, it becomes a question: "학생이에요?" (Are you a student?).
column2: 句末语调上扬就变成问句："학생이에요?" (你是学生吗？)。

column1: Write the noun and "이에요" together, with no space.
column2: 名词和 "이에요" 要连写，中间不空格。

column1: Yes, I am a student at Jeonju University.
column2: 是的，我是全州大学的学生。

column1: It means the same as "이에요/예요" but is more formal. Use it at work, in interviews, in presentations and in front of customers.
column2: 和 "이에요/예요" 意思相同，但更正式。用于工作场合、面试、发表以及在客人面前。

column1: In formal situations use "입니다"; to ask, use "입니까?".
Add "입니다" after any noun, with or without a final consonant. To ask, use "입니까?".
column2: 不管有没有韵尾，名词后面都加 "입니다"。提问时用 "입니까?"。

column1: To answer yes, say "네, 학생입니다"; to say no, use "아닙니다".
column2: 肯定回答说 "네, 학생입니다"；否定时用 "아닙니다"。

column1: In a class presentation or an interview, use the "-입니다, -습니다" style from start to finish.
column2: 在课堂发表或面试时，要从头到尾都用 "-입니다, -습니다" 的语气。

column1: Noun + 이/가 아니에요 means "is not + noun".
column2: 名词 + 이/가 아니에요 意思是 "不是 + 名词"。

column1: After a noun with a final consonant use "이 아니에요"; without one use "가 아니에요". The formal form is "아닙니다".
column2: 有韵尾的名词后用 "이 아니에요"，没有韵尾的用 "가 아니에요"。正式说法是 "아닙니다"。

column1: In English, "not" comes before the noun (not a student), but in Korean "아니에요" comes after the noun.
column2: 中文的 "不是" 放在名词前面 (不是学生)，而韩语的 "아니에요" 放在名词后面。

column1: 아니요 is the answer (no), and "아니에요" is the sentence ending (is not): "아니요, 학생이 아니에요."
column2: 아니요 是回答 (不)，"아니에요" 是句尾 (不是)："아니요, 학생이 아니에요." (不，我不是学生。)

column1: In speaking, people often drop "이/가": "학생 아니에요."
That person is not my friend.
있어요 means "have" or "be (somewhere)", and "없어요" means "don't have" or "not be (there)".
column2: 있어요 意思是 "有" 或 "在 (某处)"，"없어요" 意思是 "没有" 或 "不在"。

column1: 있다 means "have" and "be (there)"; "없다" means "don't have" and "not be (there)".
column2: 있다 意思是 "有" 和 "在"；"없다" 意思是 "没有" 和 "不在"。

column1: For things you have, say "noun + 이/가 있어요". For where something is, say "place + 에 있어요".
column2: 拥有的东西用 "名词 + 이/가 있어요"，所在的地方用 "地点 + 에 있어요"。

column1: In English, "have" and "be (somewhere)" are different words, but Korean uses "있다" for both. If there is "에", it means "be (somewhere)".
column2: 中文的 "有" 和 "在" 是两个不同的词，但韩语都用 "있다"。有 "에" 时表示 "在 (某处)"。

column1: Do not say "안 있어요" instead of "없어요".
For where a respected person is, use "계세요": "교수님은 연구실에 계세요." (The professor is in the office.)
column2: 说尊敬的人在哪里时用 "계세요"："교수님은 연구실에 계세요." (教授在办公室。)

column1: to not have, to not be there
The TA is not in the department office now.
column2: 助教现在不在系办公室。

column1: Sam, do you have time tomorrow?
Not in the morning. I have time in the afternoon.
Then let's meet in the afternoon. Where will you be?
column2: 那我们下午见吧。你会在哪里？

column1: A Korean sentence goes "who + what + do". The verb comes at the very end. This is the biggest difference from English.
column2: 韩语句子的顺序是 "谁 + 什么 + 做"。动词放在最后。这是和中文最大的不同。

column1: In Korean, the verb comes at the end of the sentence, and describing words come first.
column2: 韩语的动词放在句末，修饰语放在前面。

column1: English: I eat rice. Korean: 저는 밥을 먹어요 (I rice eat). You add particles like "은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에" after nouns to show their role in the sentence.
column2: 中文：我吃饭。韩语：저는 밥을 먹어요 (我 饭 吃)。要在名词后面加 "은/는、이/가、을/를、에" 等助词，表示它在句子中的作用。

column1: A describing word comes before the word it describes. English "a big bag" is "큰 가방" (big bag) in Korean, the same order as English.
column2: 修饰语放在被修饰的词前面。中文的 "大包" 在韩语中是 "큰 가방" (大 包)，语序和中文一样。

column1: Whose also comes first: "my house" is "제 집".
column2: 谁的 也放在前面："我的家" 是 "제 집"。

column1: I eat rice. / I have a meal.
Yesterday I bought fruit at the market.
column2: 我昨天在市场买了水果。

column1: Sam, what are you doing now?

column2: 在哪里 (动作发生的地点)

column1: In Korean, raising your voice at the end makes a question. You do not need to add "do" or change the word order as in English.
column2: 在韩语中，把句末语调上扬就成了问句。不需要像中文那样在句末加 "吗"。

column1: Raise your voice at the end to make a question; question words come before the verb.
column2: 句末上扬就成了问句；疑问词放在动词前面。

column1: -아요/어요 keeps the same form; you just raise your voice at the end. "-습니다" changes to "-습니까?". Question words (뭐 what, 어디 where, 언제 when, 누구 who, 왜 why, 어떻게 how, 얼마 how much, 몇 how many) go in the place of the thing you want to ask about.
column2: -아요/어요 形式不变，只要把句末语调上扬。"-습니다" 变成 "-습니까?"。疑问词 (뭐 什么、어디 哪里、언제 什么时候、누구 谁、왜 为什么、어떻게 怎么、얼마 多少钱、몇 几) 放在你想问的内容所在的位置。

column1: In English, the question word usually comes at the start (Where are you going?), but in Korean it comes before the verb (어디에 가요?).
column2: 中文的疑问词放在答案所在的位置 (你去哪儿？)；韩语的疑问词则放在动词前面 (어디에 가요?)。
回答以 "네" (是) 或 "아니요" (不) 开头。

column1: If someone asks with "not", like "안 가요?" (Aren't you going?), answer "네, 안 가요" if you are not going, and "아니요, 가요" if you are going.
column2: 如果用否定的方式问，比如 "안 가요?" (你不去吗？)，不去时回答 "네, 안 가요" (对，不去)，去时回答 "아니요, 가요" (不，我去)。

column1: I'm going to the restaurant. Minha, have you eaten?
column2: 我去食堂。敏夏，你吃饭了吗？

column1: 은/는 shows what you are talking about. English has no word like this. It feels like "as for …".
column2: 은/는 表示所谈论的对象 (话题)。中文没有这样的词，感觉有点像 "至于……" 或 "……嘛"。

column1: Add "은/는" after the topic you want to talk about. With a final consonant use "은"; without one use "는".
column2: 在要谈论的话题后面加 "은/는"。有韵尾用 "은"，没有韵尾用 "는"。

column1: After a noun with a final consonant, add "은". After a noun without one, add "는".
column2: 有韵尾的名词后加 "은"，没有韵尾的名词后加 "는"。

column1: It is also used to compare two things: "한국은 추워요. 싱가포르는 더워요." (Korea is cold. Singapore is hot.)
column2: 比较两样东西时也用："한국은 추워요. 싱가포르는 더워요." (韩国冷，新加坡热。)

column1: When you introduce yourself, start with "저는". From the next sentence, you can drop "저는".
column2: 自我介绍时，一开始用 "저는" 开头。从下一句开始可以省略 "저는"。

column1: You will learn the difference between "은/는" and "이/가" separately in K7.
column2: 은/는 和 "이/가" 的区别会在 K7 单独学习。

column1: I drink coffee. My younger brother/sister drinks tea.
column2: 我喝咖啡。我弟弟/妹妹喝茶。

column1: I study hotel management. And you, Minha?
column2: 我学酒店管理。敏夏你呢？

column1: 이/가 marks the subject of the sentence (who, what). English has no word like this.
column2: 이/가 表示句子的主语 (谁、什么)。中文没有这样的词。

column1: Add "이/가" after the subject. With a final consonant use "이"; without one use "가".
column2: 在主语后面加 "이/가"。有韵尾用 "이"，没有韵尾用 "가"。

column1: After a noun with a final consonant, add "이". After a noun without one, add "가". "저, 나, 누구" become "제가, 내가, 누가".
column2: 有韵尾的名词后加 "이"，没有韵尾的名词后加 "가"。"저、나、누구" 变成 "제가、내가、누가"。

column1: Before "있다, 없다, 좋다, 싫다, 아프다, 필요하다, 되다, 아니다" use "이/가": "돈이 필요해요." (I need money.)
column2: 在 "있다、없다、좋다、싫다、아프다、필요하다、되다、아니다" 前面用 "이/가"："돈이 필요해요." (我需要钱。)

column1: When someone asks "누가?" (who?), answer with "이/가": "제가 했어요". Don't say "저는 했어요".
column2: 别人问 "누가?" (谁？) 时，用 "이/가" 回答："제가 했어요"。不说 "저는 했어요"。

column1: In speaking, it is often dropped: "비 와요."
Well done. Which part was difficult?
to do well, to be good at
을/를 marks the thing that receives the action (the object). English has no word like this.
column2: 을/를 表示接受动作的对象 (宾语)。中文没有这样的词。

column1: Add "을/를" after the object of the action. With a final consonant use "을"; without one use "를".
column2: 在动作的宾语后面加 "을/를"。有韵尾用 "을"，没有韵尾用 "를"。

column1: After a noun with a final consonant, add "을". After a noun without one, add "를".
column2: 有韵尾的名词后加 "을"，没有韵尾的名词后加 "를"。

column1: English "eat rice" is "밥을 먹어요" in Korean. The object comes before the verb.
column2: 中文的 "吃饭" 在韩语中是 "밥을 먹어요" (饭 吃)。宾语放在动词前面。

column1: 무엇을 is shortened to "뭘", and "이것을" to "이걸".
column2: 무엇을 缩略为 "뭘"，"이것을" 缩略为 "이걸"。

column1: 좋아하다 (to like) takes "을/를", and "좋다" (to be good) takes "이/가": "커피를 좋아해요." "커피가 좋아요."
column2: 좋아하다 (喜欢) 用 "을/를"，"좋다" (好) 用 "이/가"："커피를 좋아해요." "커피가 좋아요."

column1: I watch a movie on the weekend.
도 is added after a noun and adds the meaning "also, too".
column2: 도 加在名词后面，表示 "也" 的意思。

column1: Add it after a noun. It goes in the place of "은/는, 이/가, 을/를". After "에, 에서" just add it (에도, 에서도).
column2: 加在名词后面。它代替 "은/는、이/가、을/를" 的位置。在 "에、에서" 后面直接加 (에도、에서도)。

column1: In English, "too" comes at the end of the sentence, but "도" comes right after the noun: "저도 가요" = I'm going too.
column2: 中文的 "也" 放在动词前面 (我也去)，而 "도" 紧跟在名词后面："저도 가요" = 我也去。

column1: 저도요 is a short answer: "Me too".
column2: 저도요 是简短的回答："我也是"。

column1: Me too. Shall we have some bread too?
column2: 我也是。我们也吃点面包吧？

column1: Sounds good. Let's order bread too.
만 means "only, just". It means only that one thing, nothing else.
column2: 만 意思是 "只，仅"。表示只有那一样，没有别的。

column1: 만 is added after a noun and adds the meaning "only that".
column2: 만 加在名词后面，表示 "只有那个" 的意思。

column1: Add it after a noun. The final consonant does not matter.
column2: 加在名词后面。和有没有韵尾无关。

column1: In English, "only" comes before the noun, but "만" comes after it: "only water" = "물만".
column2: 中文的 "只" 放在动词前面，而 "만" 放在名词后面："只要水" = "물만"。

column1: 잠깐만요 and "잠시만요" mean "Just a moment" and are used very often.
column2: 잠깐만요 和 "잠시만요" 意思是 "请稍等"，非常常用。

column1: 밖에 + a negative word has the same meaning: "물밖에 없어요" = There is only water.
column2: 밖에 + 否定词 意思相同："물밖에 없어요" = 只有水。

column1: Yes, we'll order in a little while.
column2: 是的，我们等一会儿再点。

column1: 의 means "'s" or "of". The owner comes first, like English "'s" (my friend's bag), not like "of" (the bag of my friend).
column2: 의 意思是 "的"。和中文一样，拥有者放在前面 (朋友的包)。

column1: Owner + 의 + thing. 저의 becomes "제", and 나의 becomes "내".
column2: 拥有者 + 의 + 东西。저의 变成 "제"，나의 变成 "내"。

column1: The order is "owner + 의 + thing". "저의, 나의, 너의" are shortened to "제, 내, 네".
column2: 顺序是 "拥有者 + 의 + 东西"。"저의、나의、너의" 缩略为 "제、내、네"。

column1: The particle "의" can also be pronounced [에]: 친구의 [친구에].
In speaking, "의" is often dropped: "친구 가방", "한국 음식".
column2: 说话时常省略 "의"："친구 가방" (朋友的包)、"한국 음식" (韩国菜)。

column1: When Koreans talk about their family, home, school or country, they use "우리" (our) more than "제" (my): "우리 집", "우리 학교".
column2: 韩国人谈到家人、家、学校或国家时，比起 "제" (我的)，更常用 "우리" (我们的)："우리 집"、"우리 학교"。

column1: Add "에" after a time word. It is like "at, on, in" in English.
column2: 在时间词后面加 "에"。相当于中文表示时间的 "在……" (如 "在七点")。

column1: Add "에" after time words. Don't add it to 오늘, 내일, 어제.
column2: 在时间词后面加 "에"。오늘、내일、어제 后面不加。

column1: Add it after times, days of the week, dates, months and years. The final consonant does not matter.
column2: 加在时间、星期、日期、月份和年份后面。和有没有韵尾无关。

column1: Don't add "에" after "오늘, 내일, 어제, 지금, 언제, 매일": "내일 만나요." (like English "See you tomorrow", not "on tomorrow").
column2: 오늘、내일、어제、지금、언제、매일 后面不加 "에"："내일 만나요." (就像中文说 "明天见"，不说 "在明天见")。

column1: If there are several time words, add it only to the last one: "토요일 오후 세 시에".
column2: 如果有好几个时间词，只在最后一个后面加："토요일 오후 세 시에" (星期六下午三点)。

column1: English often puts the time at the end of the sentence, but Korean puts it near the front.
column2: 和中文一样，韩语的时间一般放在句子前面。

column1: I meet a friend on Saturday.
What are you doing in the evening?
I'm going to Korea next year.
What time does your class start?
Then do you have time on the weekend?
Add "에" after the place where a person or thing is, and after the place you go to or come to.
column2: 在人或东西所在的地方，以及要去或要来的地方后面加 "에"。

column1: Add "에" after the place where something is and the place you go to.
column2: 在所在的地方和要去的地方后面加 "에"。

column1: Use "place + 에 + 있다/없다" and "place + 에 + 가다/오다/다니다".
column2: 用 "地点 + 에 + 있다/없다" 和 "地点 + 에 + 가다/오다/다니다"。

column1: In English, "to" comes before the place (go to the market), but in Korean "에" comes after it: "시장에 가요".
column2: 中文的 "去" 放在地点前面 (去市场)，而韩语的 "에" 放在地点后面："시장에 가요"。

column1: Position words (위 on/above, 아래 under, 앞 in front of, 뒤 behind, 옆 next to, 안 in, 밖 outside) come after the noun: "on the desk" = "책상 위".
column2: 方位词 (위 上、아래 下、앞 前、뒤 后、옆 旁边、안 里、밖 外) 放在名词后面，和中文一样："桌子上" = "책상 위"。

column1: 여기에, 거기에, 저기에, 어디에 can also be said without "에": "여기, 거기, 저기, 어디".
My passport is in the bag.
on the desk, top of the desk
Please come to the department office.
Add "에서" after the place where you do something. It also shows the place you come from (from).
column2: 在做事的地点后面加 "에서"。它也表示来自的地方 (从)。

column1: For where something is, use "에"; for where you do something, use "에서".
column2: 表示所在的地方用 "에"；表示做事的地方用 "에서"。

column1: Use "place + 에서 + action (먹다, 공부하다, 일하다, 사다, 만나다)".
English "at/in" becomes two forms in Korean. For where you are, use "에" (집에 있어요); for where you do something, use "에서" (집에서 쉬어요).
column2: 中文的 "在" 在韩语中分为两种形式。表示所在的地方用 "에" (집에 있어요 我在家)；表示做事的地方用 "에서" (집에서 쉬어요 我在家休息)。

column1: 살다 (to live) can take both "에" and "에서": "전주에 살아요", "전주에서 살아요".
column2: 살다 (住) 既可以用 "에"，也可以用 "에서"："전주에 살아요"、"전주에서 살아요"。

column1: In speaking, they are shortened to "여기서, 거기서, 어디서".
I work part-time at a cafe.
I study at the library in the Star Center.
column2: 我在 Star Center 的图书馆学习。

column1: (으)로 shows direction (toward), and way or tool (by, with).
column2: (으)로 表示方向 (往)，以及方式或工具 (用，坐)。

column1: After a noun with a final consonant, add "으로". After a noun with no final consonant or with a ㄹ final consonant, add "로".
column2: 有韵尾的名词后加 "으로"；没有韵尾或以 ㄹ 为韵尾的名词后加 "로"。

column1: 에 가요 is the place you arrive at; "(으)로 가요" is the direction you go in: "2층으로 올라가세요." (Go up to the 2nd floor.)

column1: Changing to something also uses "(으)로": "큰 걸로 바꿔 주세요." (Please change it to a bigger one.)
column2: 换成别的东西也用 "(으)로"："큰 걸로 바꿔 주세요." (请换成大一点的。)

column1: When you choose something, you say "이걸로 주세요" (I'll take this one).

column1: Add it after a person or an animal. In speaking use "한테", in writing use "에게", and for a respected person use "께".

column1: The giver (from) is "한테서, 에게서": "친구한테서 들었어요." In speaking, just "한테" is also fine.
column2: 给予者 (从……) 用 "한테서、에게서"："친구한테서 들었어요." (我是从朋友那里听说的。) 口语中只说 "한테" 也可以。

column1: If you use "께", the verb must also be polite. Not "주다" but "드리다": "교수님께 드렸어요."
column2: 用 "께" 时，动词也要用敬语。不是 "주다"，而是 "드리다"："교수님께 드렸어요." (我交给教授了。)

column1: 까지 is often used for deadlines: "금요일까지 내세요." (Hand it in by Friday.)

column1: 하고 is added with or without a final consonant. "와/과": "와" without a final consonant, "과" with one. "(이)랑": "이랑" with a final consonant, "랑" without one.
column2: 하고 不管有没有韵尾都可以用。"와/과"：没有韵尾用 "와"，有韵尾用 "과"。"(이)랑"：有韵尾用 "이랑"，没有韵尾用 "랑"。

column1: In speaking use "하고, (이)랑"; in writing and presentations use "와/과".
column2: 口语用 "하고、(이)랑"；书面语和发表时用 "와/과"。

column1: These words connect a noun with a noun. To connect sentences, use "-고" or "그리고".

column1: When it means "with (together)", people often add "같이" or "함께": "친구하고 같이".
column2: 表示 "和……一起" 时，常加上 "같이" 或 "함께"："친구하고 같이" (和朋友一起)。

column2: 中文的 "比" 放在比较对象的前面 (比孟加拉冷)，而韩语的 "보다" 放在比较对象的后面 (방글라데시보다 추워요)。

column1: You can use it with "더" (more) and "덜" (less): "이게 덜 매워요." (This one is less spicy.)

column1: In English, "every" comes before the noun, but "마다" comes after it: "every morning" = "아침마다".
column2: 中文的 "每" 放在名词前面，而 "마다" 放在名词后面："每天早上" = "아침마다"。

column1: 매일, 매주, 매달, 매년 mean the same as "날마다, 주마다, 달마다, 해마다".

column2: 每个人的想法都不一样。

column1: After a noun with a final consonant, add "이나". After a noun without one, add "나".
column2: 有韵尾的名词后加 "이나"，没有韵尾的名词后加 "나"。

column1: Connect nouns with "(이)나" and verbs with "-거나": "쉬거나 운동해요."
column2: 名词用 "(이)나" 连接，动词用 "-거나" 连接："쉬거나 운동해요." (休息或者运动。)

column1: After a number, it means "more than expected": "열 명이나 왔어요" = As many as 10 people came.
column2: 放在数字后面，表示 "比预想的多"："열 명이나 왔어요" = 来了足足10个人。

column1: In a question asking someone to choose one of two, use "아니면": "커피 마실래요, 아니면 차 마실래요?"
column2: 在问句中让对方二选一时，用 "아니면"："커피 마실래요, 아니면 차 마실래요?" (你要喝咖啡还是喝茶？)

column1: 처럼 means "like, as". Use it to say that something is similar to something else.

column1: Add it after a noun. The final consonant does not matter. "같이" is also used with the same meaning.

column1: In English, "like" comes before the noun, but "처럼" comes after it.
column2: 中文的 "像" 放在名词前面，而 "처럼" 放在名词后面 (相当于 "……一样")。

column1: 처럼 describes verbs and adjectives. To describe a noun, use "같은": "가족 같은 사람". "~ 같아요" means "It's like…".
column2: 처럼 修饰动词和形容词。修饰名词时用 "같은"："가족 같은 사람" (像家人一样的人)。"~ 같아요" 意思是 "像……"。

column1: When teaching cooking or sports, people often say "이렇게, 저처럼 하세요" (Do it like this, like me).
column2: 教做饭或运动时，人们常说 "이렇게, 저처럼 하세요" (这样做，像我一样做)。

column1: English does not have this difference. Use "은/는" when you talk about something already known, and "이/가" when you give new information or answer "who? what?".

column1: 은/는 is for the topic and for comparing. "이/가" is for new information and the answer to "who?".
column2: 은/는 用于话题和比较。"이/가" 用于新信息和回答 "谁"。

column1: Question words "누가, 무엇이, 어디가" and their answers use "이/가": "누가 했어요?" "제가 했어요."
column2: 疑问词 "누가、무엇이、어디가" 及其回答用 "이/가"："누가 했어요?" (谁做的？) "제가 했어요." (我做的。)

column1: The first time you mention something, use "이/가". After that, use "은/는": "저기 사람이 있어요. 그 사람은 제 룸메이트예요."
column2: 第一次提到时用 "이/가"，之后用 "은/는"："저기 사람이 있어요. 그 사람은 제 룸메이트예요." (那里有个人。那个人是我的室友。)

column1: 살다 works with both: "전주에 살아요", "전주에서 살아요".
column2: 살다 两个都可以用："전주에 살아요"、"전주에서 살아요"。

column1: Both are used for where you go, but "에" is the place you arrive at, and "(으)로" is the direction. "(으)로" is also used for routes, tools, and materials.

column1: The place you arrive at uses "에". Direction, tools, and what something changes into use "(으)로".

column1: With no final consonant or a final ㄹ, use "로". With other final consonants, use "으로": 버스로, 지하철로, 오른쪽으로.

column1: They all mean English "and, with". The meaning is the same, but where you use them is different.

column1: Use "하고" in speaking, "와/과" in writing, and "(이)랑" with close friends.

column1: With no final consonant, use "와, 랑". With a final consonant, use "과, 이랑": 친구와, 동생과, 친구랑, 동생이랑. "하고" does not change.

column1: Both mean English "because, so". But if an order or a suggestion comes after, you can only use "-(으)니까".

column1: Facts, thanks, and apologies use "-아서". Reasons for an order or a suggestion use "-(으)니까".

column2: -아서 前面不能用 "-았/었-"。不是 "아팠어서"，而是 "아파서 못 갔어요"。"-(으)니까" 前面可以用："먹었으니까"。

column1: Both mean English "but". "-지만" shows a clear contrast. "-는데" connects softly and gives background for what you say next.

column1: Before you ask or request something, first explain the situation with "-는데". It sounds polite: "길을 잘 모르는데 좀 가르쳐 주세요."

column1: Both mean English "will". "-(으)ㄹ게요" is a promise to the listener, and "-(으)ㄹ 거예요" is a plan or a guess.

column1: A promise uses "-(으)ㄹ게요". Plans and guesses use "-(으)ㄹ 거예요".

column1: -(으)ㄹ게요 is only used for "I, we", and you can't ask questions with it. "민하 씨가 할게요" and "할게요?" are wrong.

column1: When you answer an order, use "-(으)ㄹ게요" or "-겠습니다": "이거 좀 해 줘요." "네, 할게요." Here "할 거예요" sounds unnatural.

column1: Both are polite requests. "-(으)세요" suggests something for the listener, and "-아/어 주세요" asks someone to do something for me.

column1: Words for the listener's good use "-(으)세요". Requests for me use "-아/어 주세요".

column1: When it helps you, say "-아/어 주세요". "문을 여세요" sounds like an order, and "문 좀 열어 주세요" is a request.

column1: When it's good for the listener, use "-(으)세요": "많이 드세요", "쉬세요", "조심하세요". Using "주세요" here sounds unnatural.
column2: 对听话人有好处的事用 "-(으)세요" 来劝："많이 드세요" (多吃点)、"쉬세요" (休息吧)、"조심하세요" (小心)。这里用 "주세요" 不自然。

column1: After ㅏ, ㅗ use "-아요"; otherwise use "-어요"; 하다 becomes "해요".
column2: ㅏ、ㅗ 后面用 "-아요"，其他用 "-어요"，하다 变成 "해요"。

column1: Take off "-다". If the last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, add "-아요"; for other vowels add "-어요"; "하다" becomes "해요". If the stem ends in a vowel, it shortens (가+아요 → 가요, 오+아요 → 와요, 마시+어요 → 마셔요, 배우+어요 → 배워요).
column2: 去掉 "-다"。如果最后的元音是 ㅏ 或 ㅗ，加 "-아요"；其他元音加 "-어요"；"하다" 变成 "해요"。词干以元音结尾时会缩略 (가+아요 → 가요，오+아요 → 와요，마시+어요 → 마셔요，배우+어요 → 배워요)。

column1: English verbs change only a little (go, goes, went), but the endings of Korean verbs change in many ways. In the dictionary, they appear in the "-다" form.
column2: 中文的动词没有词形变化，但韩语动词的词尾有很多种变化。词典中的动词以 "-다" 的形式出现。

column1: The same form is used to tell, ask, tell someone to do something, and suggest doing it together: 가요. 가요? 빨리 가요! 같이 가요.
column2: 同一个形式可以用来陈述、提问、命令和提议一起做：가요 (我去)。가요? (你去吗？) 빨리 가요! (快走！) 같이 가요 (一起去吧)。

column1: This is the formal ending used in official situations. It is used in meetings, presentations, interviews, announcements and the news.
column2: 这是在正式场合使用的正式语尾。用于会议、发表、面试、广播通知和新闻。

column1: With a final consonant use "-습니다"; without one use "-ㅂ니다".
With a final consonant add "-습니다"; without one add "-ㅂ니다". To ask, use "-습니까?/ㅂ니까?".
column2: 有韵尾加 "-습니다"；没有韵尾加 "-ㅂ니다"。提问时用 "-습니까?/ㅂ니까?"。

column1: The ㄹ final consonant drops: 알다 → 압니다, 만들다 → 만듭니다.
column2: 韵尾 ㄹ 会脱落：알다 → 압니다，만들다 → 만듭니다。

column1: When answering a professor or a customer, "네, 알겠습니다", "감사합니다" and "죄송합니다" are always said in this style.
column2: 回答教授或客人时，"네, 알겠습니다"、"감사합니다"、"죄송합니다" 总是用这种语体。

column1: Use "-(으)세요" to show respect for what other people do. Don't use it for yourself.
column2: 尊敬别人所做的事时用 "-(으)세요"，自己的事不用。

column1: With a final consonant add "-으세요"; without one add "-세요". It is a short form of "-(으)시- + -어요".
column2: 有韵尾加 "-으세요"，没有韵尾加 "-세요"。这是 "-(으)시- + -어요" 的缩略形式。

column1: Don't use it for things you do yourself. If someone asks "어디 가세요?", answer "집에 가요". Saying "집에 가세요" is wrong.
column2: 不能用于自己做的事。别人问 "어디 가세요?" (您去哪儿？) 时，要回答 "집에 가요"。说 "집에 가세요" 是错的。

column1: Some words change completely: 먹다 → 드세요, 자다 → 주무세요, 있다 (a person is somewhere) → 계세요.
column2: 有些词会完全改变形式：먹다 → 드세요，자다 → 주무세요，있다 (人在某处) → 계세요。

column1: The same form is also used to tell someone politely to do something (앉으세요). You will learn this in H-01.
column2: 同样的形式也用于礼貌地请别人做某事 (앉으세요 请坐)。这会在 H-01 中学习。

column1: The professor is having a meal now.
I'm going to the department office. What are you doing, Sam?
column2: 我去系办公室。山姆，你在做什么？

column1: I'm going to the library. Have you had lunch?
column2: 我去图书馆。您吃过午饭了吗？

column1: This marks respect for the subject of the sentence. Add it to the actions of older people, bosses, customers and people you meet for the first time.
column2: 这是尊敬句子主语的标记。用于长辈、上司、客人以及初次见面的人的动作。

column1: For the actions of a respected person, put "-(으)시-" in the verb.
column2: 对于尊敬的人所做的事，要在动词里加 "-(으)시-"。

column1: With a final consonant put in "-으시-"; without one put in "-시-", then add the ending: 가다 → 가십니다, 가셨어요, 가실 거예요.
column2: 有韵尾加 "-으시-"，没有韵尾加 "-시-"，然后再加语尾：가다 → 가십니다，가셨어요，가실 거예요。

column1: In English you show respect with words like "sir" or "please", but in Korean you put "-시-" inside the verb.
column2: 中文用 "您"、"请" 等词表示尊敬，而韩语是在动词里面加 "-시-"。

column1: The respect is for the person who does the action. Even if you are talking to a friend, when you talk about the professor you say "교수님이 오셨어".
column2: 尊敬的对象是 "做这件事的人"。即使是在跟朋友说话，谈到教授时也要说 "교수님이 오셨어" (教授来了)。

column1: The head of the department is in class.
She is in class now. It will finish in 30 minutes.
column2: 她现在正在上课。30分钟后结束。

column1: This is the respectful form of "이/가". Use it when a respected person is the subject.
column2: 这是 "이/가" 的敬语形式。当尊敬的人是主语时使用。

column1: When a respected person is the subject, use "께서" together with "-(으)시-".
column2: 当尊敬的人是主语时，"께서" 和 "-(으)시-" 一起使用。

column1: Add it after a person and also use "-(으)시-" in the verb. The respectful form of "은/는" is "께서는", and of "도" is "께서도".
column2: 加在人的后面，动词也要同时用 "-(으)시-"。"은/는" 的敬语是 "께서는"，"도" 的敬语是 "께서도"。

column1: 께서 is used in formal speech and writing. In everyday talk, you can just use "이/가" with "-시-", as in "어머니가 요리하세요".
column2: 께서 用于正式的口语和书面语。日常对话中只用 "이/가" 加 "-시-" 也可以，比如 "어머니가 요리하세요"。

column1: It is used with respectful words: 말 → 말씀, 집 → 댁, 나이 → 연세, 이름 → 성함, 밥 → 진지, 아프다 → 편찮으시다.
column2: 和敬语词汇一起使用：말 → 말씀，집 → 댁，나이 → 연세，이름 → 성함，밥 → 진지，아프다 → 편찮으시다。

column1: The head of the department said so.
the head of the department (respectful, subject)
The staff at this shop are always kind.
column2: 这家店的店员总是很亲切。

column1: My new roommate is nice, so I'm happy.
column2: 新来的室友人很好，我很开心。

column1: It's fun to chat with friends during the break.
column2: 课间和朋友聊天很开心。

column1: The dormitory is quiet, so I sleep well.
column2: 宿舍很安静，所以我睡得很好。

column1: My younger brother is outgoing and has many friends.
column2: 我弟弟很活泼，朋友很多。

column1: Outgoing people are good at welcoming customers.
column2: 开朗的人很会接待客人。

column1: I'm hard-working, so I get up early.
I studied diligently, so I got praise.
column2: 我认真学习，所以受到了表扬。

column1: If you are lazy, it is hard to extend your contract.
column2: 如果偷懒，就很难续签合同。

column1: The shop owner is looking for a sincere part-timer.
column2: 老板在找踏实的兼职生。

column1: My older sister is warm and caring.
Minha is warm to her friends.
He is very sincere and hard-working.
Words about friends, neighbors and making friends.
column2: 关于朋友、邻居和交朋友的词。

column1: 친구 is used between people of the same age.
In Korean, "친구" usually means someone of the same age. If the age is different, even close people call each other 형, 누나, 동생.
column2: 韩语的 "친구" 通常指同龄人。年龄不同的话，即使关系很好，也互相称呼 형、누나、동생。

column1: 남자 친구 and "여자 친구" mean boyfriend and girlfriend. For a friend who is just a friend, say "남자인 친구" (a friend who is a man).
column2: 남자 친구、"여자 친구" 是男朋友、女朋友的意思。只是普通朋友时说 "남자인 친구" (是男性的朋友)。

column1: I joined this club because a friend introduced me.
column2: 我是经朋友介绍来这个社团的。

column1: I say hello to my neighbor.
My neighbor was noisy, so I couldn't sleep.
The two of them are dating.
I made a lot of friends.
I made friends at a Korean language group.
column2: 我在韩语聚会上交了朋友。

column1: I watch a movie with my boyfriend.
My boyfriend is waiting in Bangladesh.
column2: 我男朋友在孟加拉国等我。
我女朋友在乌兹别克斯坦。

column1: Please help me choose a birthday present for my girlfriend.
column2: 请帮我挑女朋友的生日礼物。
我简单地介绍一下自己。

column1: I have a close friend in Korea.
column2: 我有一个好朋友在韩国。

column1: I became close to my dorm roommate.
column2: 我和宿舍室友变得很要好。

column1: Let me introduce my friend Aisha.
column2: 我来介绍我的朋友爱莎。

column1: Nice to meet you. Are you two close?
column2: 很高兴见到你。你们俩很要好吗?

column1: Yes, we are friends from the same hometown.
column2: 是的，我们是同乡的朋友。

column1: Korean has two sets of numbers. This set is "일, 이, 삼", used for dates, money, phone numbers, floors and minutes.
column2: 韩语有两套数字。这一套是 "일, 이, 삼"，用于日期、钱、电话号码、楼层和分钟。

column1: For dates, money, numbers, floors and minutes, use "일, 이, 삼".
column2: 日期、钱、号码、楼层、分钟用 "일, 이, 삼"。

column1: Numbers are made in a regular way: 십일 (11 = ten-one), 이십 (20 = two-ten), 삼십오 (35 = three-ten-five). Unlike English "eleven" or "twenty", every number follows the rule.
column2: 这些数字来自汉字，和中文一样很有规律：십일 (十一)、이십 (二十)、삼십오 (三十五)。

column1: Big numbers are counted in units of "만" (10,000). 100,000 is "십만" (ten 만), 1,000,000 is "백만" (a hundred 만). This is different from English, which groups by thousands.
column2: 和中文一样，大数以 "만" (万) 为单位：십만 (十万)、백만 (百万)。

column1: Read phone numbers one digit at a time, and say 0 as "공".
column2: 电话号码一个数字一个数字地读，0 读作 "공"。

column1: Please go up to the 2nd floor.
Please use the restroom on the 2nd floor.
I extend my visa in three months.
column2: 三个月后我要延长签证。

column1: My room is room 602 on the 6th floor.
I get my part-time pay on the 7th of every month.
column2: 我每月七号领打工工资。

column1: Bus No. 8 stops in front of the school.
There is a test in September.
The last number of the phone number is nine.
column2: 电话号码的最后一位是九。

column1: We'll give you a ten percent discount.
What floor is the department office on?
하나, 둘, 셋 are used to count things and people, and to say the hour and age.
column2: 하나, 둘, 셋 用于数东西和人，也用于说几点和年龄。

column1: Before a counter word, they change to "한, 두, 세, 네".
column2: 在量词前变成 "한, 두, 세, 네"。

column1: Before a counter word, the form changes: 하나 → 한, 둘 → 두, 셋 → 세, 넷 → 네, 스물 → 스무. 한 개, 두 명, 세 시, 네 살, 스무 살.
column2: 在量词前形式会变化：하나 → 한、둘 → 두、셋 → 세、넷 → 네、스물 → 스무。한 개、두 명、세 시、네 살、스무 살。

column1: When telling the time, "시" uses native Korean numbers (하나, 둘…) and "분" uses Sino-Korean numbers (일, 이…): 세 시 십 분 (3:10).
column2: 说时间时，"시" (点) 用固有词数字 (하나, 둘…)，"분" (分) 用汉字词数字 (일, 이…)：세 시 십 분 (3:10)。

column1: May I ask one more thing?
column2: 我可以再问一个问题吗?

column1: The two of us go together.
The two of us lift this box together.
column2: 我们两个一起抬这个箱子。

column1: When I say one, two, three, we lift it together.
column2: 我数一、二、三，我们一起抬。

column1: Four of us share our room.
column2: 我们房间四个人一起住。

column1: Do you have a table for five?
I eat dinner at six o'clock.
I get up at seven o'clock.
You must come to the library by seven o'clock.
I start my part-time job at eight o'clock.
I sleep eight hours a day.
The bank opens at nine o'clock.
I go to bed at ten o'clock.
Please be quiet after ten o'clock.
We have to move twenty boxes.
How to say dates and days of the week. Korean goes from big to small: year, month, day.
column2: 说日期和星期的方法。韩语从大到小：年、月、日。

column1: Say dates in the order year, month, day.
column2: 日期按年、月、日的顺序说。

column1: The order is different from English: 13 November 2026 (or November 13, 2026) = 2026년 11월 13일. Korean goes year, month, day.
column2: 和中文一样，按年、月、日的顺序：2026年11月13日 = 2026년 11월 13일。

column1: June is read as "유월", and October as "시월".
It has been one year since I came to Korea.
The contract period is three years.
I go on vacation in December.
My scholarship comes in on the 25th.
There is a class on Monday mornings.
I go to the hospital on Tuesday.
There is a group meeting on Tuesday.
We throw out recycling on Tuesdays.
Wednesday is the day classes finish early.
column2: 星期三是课结束得早的日子。

column1: The head of the department prepared them himself.
Really? Please tell him thank you.
column2: 是吗？请替我谢谢系主任。

column1: This is casual speech used with close friends, younger people and family. At work, older or senior people may also use it with junior people.
column2: 这是对亲密的朋友、比自己小的人和家人使用的非敬语。在工作中，年长者或上级也可能对下级使用。

column1: Casual speech is "-아요/어요" without "요", and you use it only with people you are close to.
column2: 非敬语 (반말) 就是去掉 "-아요/어요" 中的 "요"，只在关系亲密的人之间使用。

column1: Take "요" off "-아요/어요". "이에요/예요" becomes "이야/야". "네" becomes "응", and "아니요" becomes "아니".
column2: 去掉 "-아요/어요" 的 "요"。"이에요/예요" 变成 "이야/야"。"네" 变成 "응"，"아니요" 变成 "아니"。

column1: First, learn to understand casual speech. Use it yourself only after the other person says "말 편하게 해요" or "말 놓으세요" (You can speak casually).
column2: 首先要学会听懂非敬语。自己使用时，要等对方说了 "말 편하게 해요" 或 "말 놓으세요" (说话随意点吧) 以后再用。

column1: Even if an older student (선배) or an older friend speaks casually to you, answer with "-요". Often they do not mean to be rude.
column2: 即使学长学姐 (선배) 或年长的朋友对你说非敬语，你也要用 "-요" 回答。他们往往并不是不尊重你。

column1: Some verbs don't add "-(으)시-" to show respect; they use a completely different word. It is a bit like English using "dine" instead of "eat".
column2: 有些动词表示尊敬时不加 "-(으)시-"，而是换成完全不同的词。这有点像中文把 "吃" 说成 "用餐"。

column1: Don't use these for yourself. To "많이 드세요", answer "네, 많이 먹겠습니다". "드시겠습니다" is wrong.
column2: 这些词不能用于自己。别人说 "많이 드세요" 时，要回答 "네, 많이 먹겠습니다"。"드시겠습니다" 是错的。

column1: 안녕히 가세요 is said to the person leaving, and "안녕히 계세요" to the person staying.
column2: 안녕히 가세요 是对离开的人说的，"안녕히 계세요" 是对留下的人说的。

column1: 있다 has two honorific forms. When a person "is (somewhere)", use "계시다"; when someone "has" something, use "있으시다": "시간 있으세요?"
column2: 있다 有两种敬语形式。人 "在 (某处)" 时用 "계시다"；某人 "有" 某物时用 "있으시다"："시간 있으세요?" (您有时间吗？)

column1: Please eat a lot. (Enjoy your meal.)
Professor, would you like some coffee?
My grandmother goes to bed early.
Did you sleep well last night?
The department head is in the department office now.
column2: 系主任现在在系办公室。

column1: When the professor is speaking, take notes.
Professor Im Hyeonjeong is sick, so there is no class today.
column2: 林贤贞教授身体不适，所以今天没有课。

column1: Did you have lunch? (to the TA)
Not yet. How about you, Sam?
I haven't eaten yet either. Is the professor in her office?
column2: 我也还没吃。教授在办公室吗？

column1: No, she is sick today, so she didn't come in.
column2: 不在，她今天身体不舒服，没来学校。

column1: These words make your own action toward an older or higher person humble, to show respect. The person you respect is the one who receives the action.
column2: 这些词通过谦称自己对长辈或上级的动作来表示尊敬。被尊敬的是接受动作的人。

column1: For your actions toward older or higher people, use "드리다, 여쭙다, 뵙다, 모시다, 말씀드리다".
column2: 自己对长辈或上级做的事，用 "드리다、여쭙다、뵙다、모시다、말씀드리다" 来说。

column1: Use the two kinds of respect correctly. For what an older person does, use "-(으)시-" (교수님이 주셨어요); for what you do for an older person, use the humble word (교수님께 드렸어요).
column2: 正确区分两种敬语。长辈做的事用 "-(으)시-" (교수님이 주셨어요 教授给了我)；自己为长辈做的事用谦语 (교수님께 드렸어요 我给了教授)。

column1: -아/어 주다 also becomes "-아/어 드리다". In restaurants and shops you often hear "해 드릴게요" and "가져다드리겠습니다".
column2: -아/어 주다 也要变成 "-아/어 드리다"。在餐厅和商店里常听到 "해 드릴게요"、"가져다드리겠습니다"。

column1: to give (to an older or higher person)
I gave the assignment to the professor.
On the holiday, I gave the professor some Greek coffee.
column2: 过节时，我送了教授一些希腊咖啡。
我可以问您一个问题吗？

column1: I'll ask the professor about the exam date.
column2: 考试日期我去问一下教授。

column1: I'll see you at the interview tomorrow.
to take, to escort (an older or higher person)
column2: 陪同，带 (长辈或上级) 去

column1: I took the guest to the hotel.
I live with my parents and take care of them.
column2: 我和父母住在一起，照顾他们。

column1: Please take the guest to the department office.

column2: 我已经向系主任报告了。

column1: I have something to tell you.
to give (humble) (드릴 말씀 = something to tell you)
column2: 给 (谦语) (드릴 말씀 = 要跟您说的话)

column1: I told the professor that I would be absent because I'm sick.
column2: 我告诉教授我生病了要请假。

column1: Professor, I have something to tell you.
May I ask you something about the scholarship?
column2: 我可以问您一个关于奖学金的问题吗？

column1: Of course. Give the application form to me.
column2: 当然可以。申请表交给我吧。

column1: Okay, I'll give it to you tomorrow.
These are honorific nouns used when talking about things related to older or higher people.
column2: 这些是谈论与长辈或上级有关的事物时使用的敬语名词。

column1: If you use an honorific noun, use an honorific verb too. "이름이 뭐예요?" (normal), "성함이 어떻게 되세요?" (honorific).
column2: 用了敬语名词，动词也要用敬语。"이름이 뭐예요?" (普通)，"성함이 어떻게 되세요?" (敬语)。

column1: 진지 is used for elders in the family; at school and in shops use "식사". "식사하셨어요?" (Have you eaten?) is a Korean greeting.
column2: 진지 用于家中的长辈；在学校和商店用 "식사"。"식사하셨어요?" (您吃饭了吗？) 是韩国的问候语。

column1: May I know the name of the person in charge?
column2: 能告诉我负责人的姓名吗？

column1: May I ask how old you are?
I went to the professor's house.
I was invited to the professor's house.
Excuse me, may I ask something?
I've heard a lot about you.
That is the new head of the department.
Welcome. May I have your name?
I'm Park Minha. I came to see Professor Sim Yeongguk.
column2: 我是朴敏夏。我来见沈英国教授。

column1: Yes, I'll let the professor know. Please wait here for a moment.
column2: 好的，我去告诉教授。请在这边稍等一下。

column1: Korean shows respect to the listener by using a humble word for "I". English has no humble form of "I", so practice "저" carefully.
column2: 韩语通过使用 "我" 的谦称来尊敬听话人。中文日常没有 "我" 的谦称形式，所以要认真练习 "저"。

column1: In front of older or higher people, use "저, 제가, 제, 저희" instead of "나, 내가, 내, 우리".
column2: 在长辈或上级面前，用 "저、제가、제、저희" 代替 "나、내가、내、우리"。

column1: When you speak with "-요" or "-습니다", use "저". "나는 샘입니다" sounds strange.
column2: 用 "-요" 或 "-습니다" 说话时要用 "저"。"나는 샘입니다" 听起来很奇怪。

column1: When you talk about your school or shop to guests, say "저희 학교, 저희 가게". But you don't lower your country; say "우리나라".
column2: 向客人介绍自己的学校或店时，说 "저희 학교、저희 가게"。但国家不用谦称，要说 "우리나라"。
我来自乌兹别克斯坦塔什干。

column1: to do wrong, to make a mistake
I'll give you my phone number.
Our team can do it together.
In Korean, the same greeting has three speech styles depending on the listener: formal (-습니다), soft polite (-요) and casual (반말).
column2: 在韩语中，同样的问候根据对象有三种语体：正式 (-습니다)、柔和的敬语 (-요) 和非敬语 (반말)。

column1: Greetings have three levels: formal "-습니다", soft "-요", and casual.
column2: 问候语有三个等级：正式的 "-습니다"、柔和的 "-요" 和非敬语。

column1: English "hello" is the same for everyone, but in Korean the form changes with the listener. If you are not sure which to use, use "-요".
column2: 中文的 "你好" 对谁说都差不多 (最多换成 "您好")，但韩语的形式会随听话人而变化。不确定用哪种时，就用 "-요"。

column1: To older or higher people, "미안해요, 고마워요" sounds too light. Use "죄송합니다, 감사합니다".
column2: 对长辈或上级说 "미안해요, 고마워요" 听起来太随便。要用 "죄송합니다, 감사합니다"。

column1: 안녕 is used both when meeting and when leaving, but only with friends and younger people.
column2: 안녕 见面和分别时都可以用，但只能对朋友和比自己小的人用。

column1: Hello. I'm Sam, and I'm taking this class from today.
column2: 大家好。我是山姆，从今天开始上这门课。

column1: Hello. Nice to meet you. (first meeting)
Hello. I just moved to this floor.
Thank you so much for interpreting.
Thank you for lending me the umbrella.
I'm sorry. I won't be late again.
column2: 对不起。我不会再迟到了。
不好意思。你等了很久吗？

column1: Sorry. I couldn't answer the phone.
column2: 不好意思。我没接到电话。

column1: Oh, Sam. Hello. Is the class okay for you?
column2: 啊，山姆。你好。课还听得懂吗？

column1: to be okay to do, worth doing
Sam, hi! Did you have lunch?
Questions also have three speech styles. If the listener is older or higher, also add "-(으)시-".
column2: 问句也有三种语体。如果听话人是长辈或上级，还要加上 "-(으)시-"。

column1: When you ask older or higher people, use "-(으)세요?" or "-(으)십니까?".
column2: 问长辈或上级时用 "-(으)세요?" 或 "-(으)십니까?"。

column1: When you ask about what an older or higher person does, don't just change the ending; add "-(으)시-". Say "어디 가세요?", not "어디 가요?".
column2: 问长辈或上级做的事时，不能只改语尾，还要加 "-(으)시-"。要说 "어디 가세요?"，而不是 "어디 가요?"。

column1: 어디 가세요? and "식사하셨어요?" are greetings. You don't need to answer in detail: "네, 잠깐 나가요", "네, 먹었습니다".
column2: 어디 가세요?、"식사하셨어요?" 是问候语，不需要详细回答："네, 잠깐 나가요" (是，出去一下)，"네, 먹었습니다" (是，吃过了)。

column1: Where are you going? I'll take you there.
Professor, where are you going? Shall I carry your bag?
column2: 教授，您去哪里？我帮您拿包吧？

column1: to give (polite) (-아/어 드리다 = do for someone)
column2: 给 (礼貌) (-아/어 드리다 = 为某人做)

column1: Where are you going? (to a senior)
Where are you going at this hour?
It's your day off. Where are you going?
column2: 今天是您的休息日，您去哪儿？

column1: Where are you going? Let's go together.
Have you eaten? Would you like to go together? (to the TA)
column2: 助教，您吃饭了吗？要一起去吗？

column1: Did you eat? Want to eat together?
Did you eat? Shall I make ramyeon?
Are you sick? Are you okay?
column2: 您哪里不舒服吗？没事吧？

column1: Did you fall? Are you okay?
You don't look well. Are you okay?
I'm going to the library. Where are you going?
column2: 我去图书馆。学长您去哪儿？

column1: To the department office. Did you have lunch?
column2: 去系办公室。你吃午饭了吗？

column1: Yes, I did. Have you eaten?
column2: 是的，吃过了。学长您吃了吗？

column1: Requests and instructions also have three speech styles. The more polite a request is, the longer it gets.
column2: 请求和指示也有三种语体。请求越礼貌，说得越长。

column1: Requests get more polite in this order: "줘 → 주세요 → 주십시오 → 주시겠어요?".
column2: 请求按照 "줘 → 주세요 → 주십시오 → 주시겠어요?" 的顺序越来越礼貌。

column1: When you ask an older or higher person, a question form is more polite than an order form: "-아/어 주시겠어요?", "-아/어 주실 수 있으세요?"
column2: 向长辈或上级请求时，用疑问的形式比命令的形式更礼貌："-아/어 주시겠어요?"、"-아/어 주실 수 있으세요?"

column1: Adding "죄송하지만", "실례지만" or "바쁘시겠지만" (I know you're busy, but…) before a request makes it softer.
column2: 在请求前加上 "죄송하지만"、"실례지만" 或 "바쁘시겠지만" (我知道您很忙，但……)，听起来更柔和。

column1: Could you say that again, please?
Could you close the window, please?
column2: 您能帮我关一下窗户吗？

column1: Could you say it again slowly, please?
column2: 您能慢慢地再说一遍吗？

column1: Excuse me, but please help me.
I can't read this Korean document. Please help me.
column2: 这份韩语文件我看不懂。请帮帮我。

column1: I'll come out soon. Wait a bit.
Professor, I know you're busy, but could you look at this document?
column2: 教授，我知道您很忙，能帮我看一下这份文件吗？

column1: There's no signature here. Sign it and bring it back.
column2: 这里没有签名。签好名再拿过来。

column1: Answers also change with the speech style. In class and at a part-time job, it is important to answer clearly.
column2: 回答也会随语体而变化。在课堂和打工时，清楚地回答很重要。

column1: To older or higher people answer "네, 알겠습니다"; if you didn't understand, say "잘 못 들었습니다".
column2: 对长辈或上级回答 "네, 알겠습니다"；如果没听懂，就说 "잘 못 들었습니다"。

column1: Answering an older or higher person with "응" or "어" is very rude. Always say "네" or "예".
column2: 用 "응" 或 "어" 回答长辈或上级是非常失礼的。一定要说 "네" 或 "예"。

column1: Don't say "네" if you didn't understand. Say "죄송합니다. 잘 못 들었습니다" or "다시 한번 말씀해 주십시오". Saying "네" when you don't understand causes problems later.
column2: 没听懂时不要说 "네"。要说 "죄송합니다. 잘 못 들었습니다" (对不起，我没听清楚) 或 "다시 한번 말씀해 주십시오" (请您再说一遍)。不懂却说 "네"，以后会出问题。

column1: 네 means not only "yes" but is also used to show "I'm listening". It is also the answer when someone calls your name: "샘 씨!" "네!"
column2: 네 不仅表示 "是"，还用来表示 "我在听"。别人叫你名字时也用它回答："샘 씨!" "네!"

column1: Understood. I'll do it right away.
Okay, I see. I'll do that.
column2: 好的，知道了。我会那样做。

column1: Okay. I'll come back tomorrow morning.
Got it. I'll call you when I arrive.
column2: 知道了。到了给你打电话。

column1: I don't know, I don't understand (formal)
column2: 我不知道，我不明白 (正式)

column1: I'm sorry. I don't really understand.
I don't know this word. Please explain it again.
column2: 这个单词我不知道。请再解释一遍。

column1: No. I'm not the one who did it.
Yes, that's right. The application details are correct.
column2: 是的，没错。申请表的内容是对的。

column1: Take this coffee to table 3 and give it to the customer. Got it?
column2: 把这杯咖啡端到3号桌给客人。明白了吗？

column1: I'm sorry. I didn't catch which table.
column2: 对不起，我没听清是几号桌。

column1: This is practice changing words with the same meaning for different listeners. The speech style depends on age, your relationship and how close you are.
column2: 练习根据听话人改变意思相同的话。语体取决于年龄、关系和亲密程度。

column1: Use the formal style with professors and guests, "-요" with seniors and new classmates, and casual speech only with close friends.
column2: 对教授和客人用正式语体，对学长学姐和刚认识的同学用 "-요"，只对亲密的朋友用非敬语。

column1: With people you meet for the first time, use "-요" whatever their age. Use casual speech only after the other person says "말 편하게 해요".
column2: 对初次见面的人，不管年龄大小都用 "-요"。要等对方说 "말 편하게 해요" 以后再用非敬语。

column1: At Korean universities, who entered first (학번, entry year) often matters more than age. Even if they are younger, use polite speech with seniors.
column2: 在韩国大学，入学先后 (학번，入学年份) 往往比年龄更重要。即使学长学姐比你年纪小，也要对他们用敬语。

column1: thank you for your hard work (formal)
Thank you for your hard work today too.
Everyone, thank you for your hard work.
Thank you for your hard work today. (to the TA)
good work (said to someone younger or lower)
column2: 辛苦了 (对晚辈或下级说)

column1: Good work, everyone. See you tomorrow.
Thank you for your hard work. I'll be going now.
to work hard (수고하셨습니다 = thank you for your hard work)
I have a class tomorrow morning, so I'll be going now.
column2: 我明天早上有课，先走了。

column1: I have plans, so I'll go first.
It's time for my bus, so I'll go first.
column2: 我的公交车快到了，先走了。

column1: I'm tired, so I'm going first.
I'm younger, so please speak casually to me.
column2: 我年纪小，请对我说话随意点吧。

column1: Please feel free to speak casually.
You're older than me, so please speak casually.
column2: 您比我年纪大，请对我说话随意点吧。

column1: I'll be going now. Thank you for your hard work. (to the TA)
(먼저 가 보겠습니다 = I'll leave first, said when leaving before others)
column2: (먼저 가 보겠습니다 = 我先走了，比别人先离开时说)

column1: Okay, good work. See you tomorrow.
Minha, I'm off. See you tomorrow.
Used to talk about the past. English uses a past form of the verb (worked, went); Korean puts "-았/었-" in the verb.
column2: 用来谈论过去。中文用 "了"、"过" 等来表示，韩语则是在动词里加 "-았/었-"。

column1: For past events, put "-았/었-" in the verb.
column2: 过去的事要在动词里加 "-았/었-"。

column1: It follows the same rule as "-아요/어요". After ㅏ, ㅗ use "-았어요"; otherwise use "-었어요"; 하다 becomes "했어요". For nouns use "이었어요/였어요".
column2: 规则和 "-아요/어요" 一样。ㅏ、ㅗ 后面用 "-았어요"，其他用 "-었어요"，하다 变成 "했어요"。名词用 "이었어요/였어요"。

column1: Even with words like "어제", you must change the verb. "어제 가요" is wrong; "어제 갔어요" is right. (Just like "Yesterday I go" is wrong in English.)
column2: 即使有 "어제" (昨天) 这样的词，动词也一定要变。"어제 가요" 是错的，"어제 갔어요" 才是对的。(就像中文要说 "昨天去了"，加上 "了"。)

column1: The formal form is "-았습니다/었습니다": 했습니다, 갔습니다.
아직 안 했어요 means "I haven't done it yet", and "벌써 했어요" means "I already did it".
column2: 아직 안 했어요 意思是 "我还没做"，"벌써 했어요" 意思是 "我已经做了"。

column1: I came to Korea last year.
Sam, why didn't you come to class yesterday?
column2: 山姆，你昨天为什么没来上课？

column1: I'm sorry. I was very sick.
Did you go to the hospital?
Yes, I did. I took medicine too.
Used to talk about things you will do or plans. It is like "will, be going to" in English. It is also used for guesses (probably will).
column2: 用来谈论将要做的事或计划。相当于中文的 "会、要、打算"。也用于推测 (大概会)。

column1: Talk about things you will do with "-(으)ㄹ 거예요".
column2: 将要做的事用 "-(으)ㄹ 거예요" 来说。

column1: With a final consonant add "-을 거예요"; without one add "-ㄹ 거예요". With a ㄹ final consonant, just add "거예요".
column2: 有韵尾加 "-을 거예요"，没有韵尾加 "-ㄹ 거예요"。以 ㄹ 为韵尾时，直接加 "거예요"。

column1: In English, "will" comes before the verb, but in Korean it is added after it: "will go" = "갈 거예요".
column2: 中文的 "要/会" 放在动词前面，而韩语是加在动词后面："要去" = "갈 거예요"。

column1: 거예요 is pronounced [꺼예요]: 갈 거예요 [갈 꺼예요] (gal kkeoyeyo).
column2: 거예요 读作 [꺼예요]：갈 거예요 [갈 꺼예요] (gal kkeoyeyo)。

column1: The formal form is "-(으)ㄹ 것입니다, -(으)ㄹ 겁니다".
What will you do on the weekend?
I'm going to my hometown next year.
What will you do this vacation?
column2: 这个假期你打算做什么？

column1: I'm going to Nepal. I will see my family.
column2: 我要去尼泊尔。我要去见家人。

column1: That's great. When will you come back?
I'll come back in two weeks.
Tells what you are doing right now. It is like "be + -ing" in English.
column2: 表示现在正在做的事。相当于中文的 "正在……"。
动词 + -고 있어요 意思是 "正在 + 动词"。

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-고 있어요". The final consonant does not matter. The respectful form is "-고 계세요".
column2: 去掉动词的 "-다"，加上 "-고 있어요"。和有没有韵尾无关。敬语形式是 "-고 계세요"。

column1: In Korean, "-아요/어요" alone can also show what you are doing now. "뭐 해요?" and "뭐 하고 있어요?" are almost the same.
column2: 在韩语中，只用 "-아요/어요" 也可以表示正在做的事。"뭐 해요?" 和 "뭐 하고 있어요?" 几乎一样。

column1: Verbs for wearing also show the state of wearing something. "모자를 쓰고 있어요" means you are putting on a hat, or you are already wearing one.
column2: 表示穿戴的动词也表示穿着的状态。"모자를 쓰고 있어요" 意思是正在戴帽子，或者已经戴着帽子。

column1: I'm studying at the library now.
column2: 我现在正在图书馆学习。

column1: She's looking for a book in the library.
It has two meanings: ① the speaker's intention (will) ② a guess (must be, it seems). It is also found in many set greetings.
column2: 有两个意思：① 说话人的意志 (要、会) ② 推测 (一定是、看起来)。很多固定的问候语里也有它。

column1: -겠- shows the speaker's intention and a guess.
column2: -겠- 表示说话人的意志和推测。

column1: Take "-다" off a verb or adjective, put in "-겠-", then add the ending. The final consonant does not matter.
column2: 去掉动词或形容词的 "-다"，加上 "-겠-"，再加语尾。和有没有韵尾无关。

column1: 알겠습니다 is the most common answer when you get an instruction. "알아요" means "I already know", so it sounds rude as an answer to an instruction.
column2: 알겠습니다 是接到指示时最常用的回答。"알아요" 意思是 "我早就知道了"，作为对指示的回答听起来很没礼貌。

column1: Set greetings: 처음 뵙겠습니다 (Nice to meet you), 잘 먹겠습니다 (Thank you for the food), 다녀오겠습니다 (I'll be back), 실례하겠습니다 (Excuse me).
column2: 固定的问候语：처음 뵙겠습니다 (初次见面)，잘 먹겠습니다 (我开动了)，다녀오겠습니다 (我出门了)，실례하겠습니다 (打扰了)。

column1: Thank you for the food. (said before eating)

column2: (我) 会来，(他/她) 大概会来

column1: This assignment has to be handed in by today.
Yes, I understand. I'll do it.
It must be hard to do it alone. Do it with Aisha.
column2: 一个人做一定很辛苦。和爱莎一起做吧。

column1: It is used in two ways: ① to suggest trying something (try … and see) ② to talk about experience (have done).
column2: 有两种用法：① 建议尝试某事 (……看看) ② 谈论经历 (做过)。

column1: -아/어 보세요 means "try … and see", and "-아/어 봤어요" means "have (done)…".
column2: -아/어 보세요 意思是 "……看看"，"-아/어 봤어요" 意思是 "……过"。

column1: Take "요" off the "-아요/어요" form and add "보다": 먹어 보세요 (try eating it), 먹어 봤어요 (I have eaten it).
column2: 去掉 "-아요/어요" 形式中的 "요"，加上 "보다"：먹어 보세요 (尝尝看)，먹어 봤어요 (我吃过)。

column1: The idea is the same as English "try … and see". "보다" means "see".
column2: 意思和中文的 "……看看" 一样。"보다" 本来的意思就是 "看"。

column1: 아직 안 해 봤어요 means "I haven't tried it yet".
column2: 아직 안 해 봤어요 意思是 "我还没试过"。

column1: Don't use it with "보다" itself. Don't say "봐 봤어요"; say "봤어요" or "본 적이 있어요".
column2: 不能和 "보다" 本身一起用。不说 "봐 봤어요"，要说 "봤어요" 或 "본 적이 있어요"。

column1: No, I haven't tried it yet.
Says whether you have or have not done something up to now. It is like "have ever (done)" in English.
column2: 表示到现在为止有没有做过某事。相当于中文的 "……过"。

column1: -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다/없다 means "have ever / have never".
column2: -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다/없다 意思是 "……过 / 从没……过"。

column1: With a final consonant add "-은 적이 있어요"; without one add "-ㄴ 적이 있어요". If you have not, use "-(으)ㄴ 적이 없어요".
column2: 有韵尾加 "-은 적이 있어요"，没有韵尾加 "-ㄴ 적이 있어요"。没做过时用 "-(으)ㄴ 적이 없어요"。

column1: In English, "have ever" comes before the verb, but in Korean it is added after it: "have been there" = "간 적이 있어요".
column2: 和中文的 "过" 一样，韩语也是加在动词后面："去过" = "간 적이 있어요"。

column1: It is often asked in (part-time) job interviews: "아르바이트를 한 적이 있습니까?" (Have you ever had a part-time job?), "커피를 만들어 본 적이 있습니까?" (Have you ever made coffee?).
column2: (打工) 面试时经常会问："아르바이트를 한 적이 있습니까?" (你打过工吗？)，"커피를 만들어 본 적이 있습니까?" (你做过咖啡吗？)。

column1: Don't use it for things you do every day. "밥을 먹은 적이 있어요" sounds strange.
column2: 不用于每天都做的事。"밥을 먹은 적이 있어요" (我吃过饭) 听起来很奇怪。

column1: I have worked part-time at a cafe.
Have you ever been to Korea?
Have you ever used this program?
Have you ever worked at a cafe?
Yes, I worked at one in the USA for a year.
column2: 是的，我在美国做过一年。

column1: Have you ever worked at a cafe in Korea?
column2: 您在韩国的咖啡店工作过吗？

column1: No, I haven't. This is my first time.
안 means "not, don't". It means you don't do something or something is not so.
column2: 안 意思是 "不"。表示不做某事或不是那样。

column1: 안 + verb means "not + verb". "Noun + 하다" becomes "noun + 안 해요".
column2: 안 + 动词 意思是 "不 + 动词"。"名词 + 하다" 变成 "名词 + 안 해요"。

column1: Put "안" right before the verb or adjective. With "noun + 하다" verbs, put it between the noun and "하다" (공부 안 해요).
column2: 把 "안" 放在动词或形容词的正前方。"名词 + 하다" 类动词，要放在名词和 "하다" 之间 (공부 안 해요)。

column1: Like English "don't + verb", "안" comes before the verb, so it is easy. But the object comes before "안": "don't eat rice" = "밥을 안 먹어요".
column2: 和中文的 "不 + 动词" 一样，"안" 放在动词前面，所以很容易。但宾语要放在 "안" 前面："不吃饭" = "밥을 안 먹어요"。

column1: For "있다" say "없어요", not "안 있어요"; for "알다" say "몰라요", not "안 알아요"; for "이다" say "아니에요".
column2: 있다 要说 "없어요"，不说 "안 있어요"；"알다" 要说 "몰라요"，不说 "안 알아요"；"이다" 要说 "아니에요"。

column1: I didn't work my part-time job yesterday.
It means "not", the same as "안". It is a little more formal and used a lot in writing.
column2: 意思是 "不"，和 "안" 一样。稍微正式一点，常用于书面语。

column1: -지 않다 means the same as "안" and is more formal.
column2: -지 않다 和 "안" 意思相同，更正式一些。

column1: Take "-다" off a verb or adjective and add "-지 않아요". The final consonant does not matter.
column2: 去掉动词或形容词的 "-다"，加上 "-지 않아요"。和有没有韵尾无关。

column1: 않아요 is pronounced [아나요] (anayo). The ㅎ is silent.
For the past, change "않다": "-지 않았어요". "갔지 않아요" is wrong.
column2: 过去的事要改变 "않다"："-지 않았어요"。"갔지 않아요" 是错的。

column1: With long words or "noun + 하다", "-지 않다" sounds more natural: "필요하지 않아요".
column2: 长的单词或 "名词 + 하다" 用 "-지 않다" 更自然："필요하지 않아요" (不需要)。

column1: 못 means you want to do something but cannot. It is like "can't" in English.
column2: 못 表示想做但做不了。相当于中文的 "不能，没法"。
못 + 动词 意思是 "不能 + 动词"。

column1: Put it right before the verb. "Noun + 하다" becomes "noun + 못 해요".
column2: 放在动词的正前方。"名词 + 하다" 变成 "名词 + 못 해요"。

column1: Like English "can't", "못" comes before the verb: "can't go" = "못 가요".
column2: 和中文的 "不能" 一样，"못" 放在动词前面："不能去" = "못 가요"。

column1: 안 가요 means you don't go because you don't want to; "못 가요" means you can't go because of some reason. When saying no, "못 가요" sounds softer.
column2: 안 가요 表示因为不想去所以不去；"못 가요" 表示因为某种原因去不了。拒绝时说 "못 가요" 更委婉。

column1: The sound changes: 못 해요 [모태요] (motaeyo), 못 먹어요 [몬머거요] (monmeogeoyo), 못 가요 [몯까요] (motkkayo).
column2: 发音会变化：못 해요 [모태요] (motaeyo)，못 먹어요 [몬머거요] (monmeogeoyo)，못 가요 [몯까요] (motkkayo)。

column1: I was sick yesterday, so I couldn't go.
column2: 我昨天病了，所以没能去。

column1: I'm not good at Korean yet.
to be bad at, can't do well
It means the same as "못". It is a little more formal and used a lot in writing.
column2: 和 "못" 意思相同。稍微正式一点，常用于书面语。

column1: -지 못하다 means the same as "못" and is more formal.
column2: -지 못하다 和 "못" 意思相同，更正式一些。

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-지 못해요".
It is often used when you hand in an assignment late or apologize: "죄송합니다. 끝내지 못했습니다." (I'm sorry. I couldn't finish it.)
column2: 迟交作业或道歉时常用："죄송합니다. 끝내지 못했습니다." (对不起，我没能完成。)

column1: It is usually not used with adjectives. Don't say "춥지 못해요"; say "춥지 않아요".
column2: 一般不用于形容词。不说 "춥지 못해요"，要说 "춥지 않아요"。

column1: I couldn't finish all the assignment.
Sam, did you finish writing the report?
I'm sorry. I haven't finished it yet.
My laptop broke down, so I couldn't write it yesterday.
column2: 我的笔记本电脑坏了，所以昨天没能写。

column1: to happen, to occur (고장 나다 = to break down)
Says whether you are able to, or have the chance to, do something. It is like "can / can't" in English.
column2: 表示有没有能力或机会做某事。相当于中文的 "能 / 不能"。

column1: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 means "can", and "-(으)ㄹ 수 없다" means "can't".
column2: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 意思是 "能"，"-(으)ㄹ 수 없다" 意思是 "不能"。

column1: With a final consonant add "-을 수 있어요"; without one add "-ㄹ 수 있어요".
column2: 有韵尾加 "-을 수 있어요"，没有韵尾加 "-ㄹ 수 있어요"。

column1: In English, "can" comes before the verb, but in Korean "수 있어요" comes at the end: "can do" = "할 수 있어요".
column2: 中文的 "能" 放在动词前面，而韩语的 "수 있어요" 放在句末："能做" = "할 수 있어요"。

column1: 수 is pronounced [쑤]: 할 수 있어요 [할 쑤 이써요] (hal ssu isseoyo).
column2: 수 读作 [쑤]：할 수 있어요 [할 쑤 이써요] (hal ssu isseoyo)。

column1: For skills you have learned, you can also say "-(으)ㄹ 줄 알아요/몰라요": "운전할 줄 알아요." (I know how to drive.)
column2: 学会的技能也可以用 "-(으)ㄹ 줄 알아요/몰라요" 来说："운전할 줄 알아요." (我会开车。)

column1: Can I use a card here?
Yes, I can speak a little.
Can you work on weekends too?
No, I can't on weekends. I can work on weekday evenings.
column2: 不，周末不行。工作日的晚上可以。

column1: Says what you want to do. It is like "want to" in English.
column2: 表示想做的事。相当于中文的 "想"。
动词 + -고 싶어요 意思是 "想 + 动词"。

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-고 싶어요". The final consonant does not matter.
column2: 去掉动词的 "-다"，加上 "-고 싶어요"。和有没有韵尾无关。

column1: In English, "want to" comes before the verb, but in Korean it is added after it: "want to go" = "가고 싶어요".
column2: 中文的 "想" 放在动词前面，而韩语是加在动词后面："想去" = "가고 싶어요"。

column1: Use it only for your own wishes and the listener's. For other people's wishes, use "-고 싶어 해요": "동생이 한국에 오고 싶어 해요." (My younger brother wants to come to Korea.)
column2: 只用于自己和听话人的愿望。别人的愿望要用 "-고 싶어 해요"："동생이 한국에 오고 싶어 해요." (我弟弟想来韩国。)

column1: 보고 싶어요 is often used to mean "I miss (you)".
column2: 보고 싶어요 常用来表示 "我想你"。

column1: I want to work at a hotel.
to see (보고 싶다 = to miss, want to see)
I don't want to do anything today.
Sam, what do you want to do after graduation?
column2: 山姆，毕业后你想做什么？

column1: I want to work at a hotel. And I want to help my family.
column2: 我想在酒店工作。还有，我想帮助家人。

column1: Which country do you want to work in?
Used to say casually what you will do, or to ask what the listener wants to do. It is used between people who are close.
column2: 用于随意地说自己要做什么，或问听话人想做什么。用于关系亲近的人之间。

column1: -(으)ㄹ래요 is used between close people to say what you want or to ask what the other person wants.
column2: -(으)ㄹ래요 用于亲近的人之间，说自己的意愿或问对方的意愿。

column1: With a final consonant add "-을래요"; without one add "-ㄹ래요".
Don't use it to tell a senior person what you want. Saying "저는 갈래요" to a professor sounds rude. Say "가겠습니다".
column2: 不能用来向长辈或上级说自己的意愿。对教授说 "저는 갈래요" 听起来没礼貌。要说 "가겠습니다"。

column1: To ask a senior person, use "-(으)시겠어요?": "뭐 드시겠어요?"
column2: 问长辈或上级时用 "-(으)시겠어요?"："뭐 드시겠어요?" (您想吃什么？)

column1: This is what you hear most when choosing food at a restaurant: "뭐 먹을래요?"
column2: 这是在餐厅点菜时最常听到的话："뭐 먹을래요?" (你要吃什么？)

column1: What do you want to drink?
Do you want to go together?
Do you want to do it?
I'll have kimchi stew. And you, Minha?
column2: 我要吃泡菜汤。敏夏你呢？

column1: I'll have soybean paste stew. Do you want a drink too?
column2: 我要吃大酱汤。你也要喝饮料吗？

column1: Used when you promise the listener you will do something. It feels like "I'll … (for you)".
column2: 用于向听话人承诺自己会做某事。感觉像 "我来 (为你) ……"。

column1: -(으)ㄹ게요 is a promise that you will do something.
column2: -(으)ㄹ게요 是承诺自己会做某事的话。

column1: With a final consonant add "-을게요"; without one add "-ㄹ게요". The subject is always "I".
column2: 有韵尾加 "-을게요"，没有韵尾加 "-ㄹ게요"。主语总是 "我"。

column1: It is not used in questions. "할게요?" is wrong.
column2: 不用于问句。"할게요?" 是错的。

column1: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is your own plan, and "-(으)ㄹ게요" is a promise made with the listener in mind: "내일 갈 거예요" (plan), "내일 갈게요" (promise).
column2: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 是自己的计划，"-(으)ㄹ게요" 是考虑到听话人而做的承诺："내일 갈 거예요" (计划)，"내일 갈게요" (承诺)。

column1: I'll be going now. (I'm leaving first.)
Thank you for the food. (said when someone treats you)
column2: 那我就不客气了。(别人请客时说)

column1: Who will take this box to the department office?
column2: 谁来把这个箱子拿到系办公室？

column1: Thanks. It's heavy, so be careful.
Used to suggest doing something together (Shall we …?) or to ask if you should do something (Shall I …?).
column2: 用于提议一起做某事 (我们……吧？) 或询问自己是否应该做某事 (要我……吗？)。

column1: -(으)ㄹ까요? is used to suggest doing something together or to ask if you should do something.
column2: -(으)ㄹ까요? 用于提议一起做某事，或询问要不要由自己来做。

column1: With a final consonant add "-을까요?"; without one add "-ㄹ까요?".
Answer with "네, 좋아요", "-(으)ㅂ시다" or "-아/어요". If you don't want to, say no softly, like "미안해요, 오늘은 좀…".
column2: 回答用 "네, 좋아요"、"-(으)ㅂ시다" 或 "-아/어요"。不想的话，要委婉地说，比如 "미안해요, 오늘은 좀…" (不好意思，今天有点……)。

column1: 제가 ~(으)ㄹ까요? asks if there is something for you to do. At a part-time job or in a group project, people often ask "뭘 할까요?" (What shall I do?).
column2: 제가 ~(으)ㄹ까요? 是询问有没有自己可以做的事。打工或做小组作业时，人们常问 "뭘 할까요?" (我做什么好？)。

column1: Shall we watch a movie together on the weekend?
column2: 周末我们一起看电影吧？

column1: Sounds good. Where shall we meet?
Shall we meet in front of the station at 2?
column2: 两点在车站前见怎么样？

column1: Used to suggest doing something together. It is like "Let's …" in English.
column2: 用于提议一起做某事。相当于中文的 "……吧"。

column1: -(으)ㅂ시다 means "Let's …", and it is not used with senior people.
column2: -(으)ㅂ시다 意思是 "……吧"，不能对长辈或上级使用。

column1: With a final consonant add "-읍시다"; without one add "-ㅂ시다". The casual form is "-자".
column2: 有韵尾加 "-읍시다"，没有韵尾加 "-ㅂ시다"。非敬语形式是 "-자"。

column1: Don't use it with senior people. To a professor, say "가시지요" or "같이 가시겠어요?".
column2: 不能对长辈或上级使用。对教授要说 "가시지요" 或 "같이 가시겠어요?"。

column1: Professors and club leaders (선배) often use it when speaking to a group: "자, 시작합시다" (OK, let's start), "조용히 합시다" (Let's be quiet).
column2: 教授或社团学长学姐 (선배) 对一群人讲话时常用："자, 시작합시다" (好，我们开始吧)，"조용히 합시다" (大家安静一下)。

column1: In normal conversation, "-아요/어요" like "같이 가요" sounds softer.
column2: 在普通对话中，像 "같이 가요" 这样用 "-아요/어요" 更柔和。

column1: Everyone, let's finish today's practice here.
column2: 各位，今天的练习就到这里吧。

column1: OK, thank you for your hard work.
Let's tidy up and go have dinner together.
column2: 我们收拾一下，一起去吃晚饭吧。

column1: Tells what you intend to do. It is like "plan to, be going to" in English.
column2: 表示打算做的事。相当于中文的 "打算，准备"。

column1: With a final consonant add "-으려고 해요"; with no final consonant or a ㄹ final consonant add "-려고 해요".
column2: 有韵尾加 "-으려고 해요"；没有韵尾或韵尾是 ㄹ 时加 "-려고 해요"。

column1: -(으)려고 했어요 often means you were going to do something but didn't.
column2: -(으)려고 했어요 常常表示本来打算做但没做成。

column1: It is also used for something about to happen: "비가 오려고 해요" = It's about to rain.
column2: 也用于即将发生的事："비가 오려고 해요" = 快要下雨了。

column1: In speaking, it is shortened to "-(으)려고요": "어디 가요?" "은행에 가려고요." (Where are you going? To the bank.)
column2: 说话时缩略为 "-(으)려고요"："어디 가요?" "은행에 가려고요." (你去哪儿？我想去银行。)

column1: I plan to go to Korea next year.
I plan to rest at home on the weekend.
I plan to save money and buy a laptop.
column2: 我打算攒钱买一台笔记本电脑。

column1: I was going to call, but I forgot.
column2: 我本来想打电话的，但忘了。

column1: What will you do when you graduate?
I plan to go back to Myanmar and open a shop.
column2: 我打算回缅甸开一家店。

column1: I plan to run a Korean restaurant.
column2: 我打算开一家韩国餐厅。

column1: It means you have agreed or promised to do something. It is like "decide to, agree to" in English.
column2: 表示已经决定或约好要做某事。相当于中文的 "决定，约好"。
-기로 했어요 意思是 "决定 / 约好……"。

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-기로 했어요". The final consonant does not matter.
column2: 去掉动词的 "-다"，加上 "-기로 했어요"。和有没有韵尾无关。

column1: Because it has already been decided, it is usually used in the past form, like "-기로 했어요".
column2: 因为是已经决定的事，所以一般用过去式 "-기로 했어요"。

column1: -(으)려고 해요 is a plan in your mind, and "-기로 했어요" is something already decided or promised with another person.
column2: -(으)려고 해요 是自己心里的打算，"-기로 했어요" 是已经决定了或和别人约好的事。

column1: For deciding not to do something, use "안 -기로 했어요" or "-지 않기로 했어요".
column2: 决定不做某事用 "안 -기로 했어요" 或 "-지 않기로 했어요"。

column1: We agreed to meet on the weekend.
I decided to live in the dormitory for one more year.
column2: 我决定在宿舍再住一年。

column1: Let's agree to have the group meeting tomorrow.
column2: 我们就定在明天开小组会吧。

column1: What are you doing on Sunday?
Aisha and I are going to play soccer. (We agreed to.)
column2: 我和爱莎约好去踢足球。

column1: Of course. We agreed to meet at the sports field at 10.
column2: 当然。我们约好十点在运动场见。

column1: A soft way to suggest doing something. It is like "How about …?" or "Why don't you …?" in English.
column2: 委婉地提议做某事。相当于中文的 "……怎么样？" 或 "不如……吧？"。

column1: -는 게 어때요? is a soft way to suggest something.
column2: -는 게 어때요? 是委婉的提议。

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-는 게 어때요?". The final consonant does not matter. A ㄹ final consonant drops (만들다 → 만드는 게).
column2: 去掉动词的 "-다"，加上 "-는 게 어때요?"。和有没有韵尾无关。韵尾 ㄹ 会脱落 (만들다 → 만드는 게)。

column1: 게 is a short form of "것이". The formal form is "-는 것이 어떻습니까?".
column2: 게 是 "것이" 的缩略形式。正式说法是 "-는 것이 어떻습니까?"。

column1: For a stronger suggestion, say "-는 게 좋겠어요": "병원에 가는 게 좋겠어요." (You'd better go to the hospital.)
column2: 更强烈地建议时说 "-는 게 좋겠어요"："병원에 가는 게 좋겠어요." (你最好去医院。)
名词用 "名词 + 어때요?"："삼겹살 어때요?" (五花肉怎么样？)

column1: How about going to see a doctor?
My lower back keeps hurting these days.
Then you'd better tell your part-time job boss and take a day off.
column2: 那你最好跟打工的老板说一声，休息一天。

column1: Used to tell or advise someone politely. It is like "Please …" in English.
column2: 用于礼貌地让别人做某事或给出建议。相当于中文的 "请……"。

column1: -(으)세요 is a polite way to tell or advise someone to do something.
column2: -(으)세요 是礼貌地让别人做某事或劝别人做某事的说法。

column1: With a final consonant add "-으세요"; without one add "-세요". A ㄹ final consonant drops (만들다 → 만드세요).
column2: 有韵尾加 "-으세요"，没有韵尾加 "-세요"。韵尾 ㄹ 会脱落 (만들다 → 만드세요)。

column1: In English, "please" comes before the verb, but in Korean the end of the verb changes: "Please sit down" = "앉으세요".
column2: 中文的 "请" 放在动词前面，而韩语是改变动词的词尾："请坐" = "앉으세요"。

column1: Use it to suggest something good for the listener. When you ask someone to do something for you, "-아/어 주세요" is more polite.
column2: 用于建议对听话人有好处的事。请别人为自己做某事时，用 "-아/어 주세요" 更礼貌。

column1: 먹다, 마시다 become "드세요", 자다 becomes "주무세요", and 있다 becomes "계세요".
column2: 먹다、마시다 变成 "드세요"，자다 变成 "주무세요"，있다 变成 "계세요"。

column1: Please write your name here. And please wait a moment.
column2: 请在这里写上名字。然后请稍等。

column1: Used when you ask someone to do something for you. It is like "Please … (for me)" in English.
column2: 用于请别人为自己做某事。相当于中文的 "请 (为我) ……"。

column1: -아/어 주세요 is a request to do something for you.
column2: -아/어 주세요 是请别人为自己做某事的说法。

column1: Take "요" off the "-아요/어요" form and add "주세요". For nouns, use "noun + 주세요".
column2: 去掉 "-아요/어요" 形式中的 "요"，加上 "주세요"。名词用 "名词 + 주세요"。

column1: 주다 means "to give". After a verb, it means doing something for someone: "도와 주다" = to help (someone).
column2: 주다 意思是 "给"。放在动词后面表示为别人做某事："도와 주다" = 帮 (某人)。
加上 "좀" 更柔和："좀 도와주세요." (请帮我一下。)

column1: More polite forms are "-아/어 주시겠어요?" and "-아/어 주실 수 있어요?".
column2: 更礼貌的说法是 "-아/어 주시겠어요?"、"-아/어 주실 수 있어요?"。

column1: Learn these three phrases for when you don't understand: "다시 말해 주세요", "천천히 말해 주세요", "써 주세요".
column2: 一定要记住听不懂时用的三句话："다시 말해 주세요" (请再说一遍)，"천천히 말해 주세요" (请说慢一点)，"써 주세요" (请写下来)。

column1: Professor, I'm sorry, but please say that again.
column2: 教授，对不起，请您再说一遍。

column1: Write this word in your notebook three times.
column2: 请在笔记本上把这个单词写三遍。

column1: Yes, I understand. Please show me once.
column2: 好的，明白了。请给我示范一次。

column1: You can write it like this.
This is the most formal way to tell someone to do something. It is used in notices, safety signs, announcements and when speaking to customers.
column2: 这是最正式的让别人做某事的说法。用于通知、安全标志、广播以及对客人说话。

column1: -(으)십시오 is the most formal way to tell someone to do something, used on signs and in announcements.
column2: -(으)십시오 是标志和广播中使用的最正式的命令形式。

column1: With a final consonant add "-으십시오"; without one add "-십시오".
-십시오 is pronounced [십씨오] (sipsio). In writing it ends in "-시오". Writing "-십시요" is wrong.
column2: -십시오 读作 [십씨오] (sipsio)。书写时以 "-시오" 结尾。写成 "-십시요" 是错的。

column1: To tell someone not to do something, use "-지 마십시오": "들어가지 마십시오." (Please do not enter.)
column2: 叫别人不要做某事时用 "-지 마십시오"："들어가지 마십시오." (请勿入内。)

column1: Notices at school and in the dorm, and subway announcements, almost always use this style. It is important to read and understand them.
column2: 学校和宿舍的通知、地铁广播几乎都用这种语体。能读懂、听懂很重要。

column1: Please exit through the emergency exit.
Please be quiet inside the library.
column2: 在图书馆内请保持安静。

column1: Do not bring food into the reading room.
column2: 请勿携带食物进入阅览室。

column1: to have, to hold (가지고 = with, carrying)
Aisha, did you turn off your phone?
Used to tell someone politely not to do something. It is like "Please don't …" in English.
column2: 用于礼貌地叫别人不要做某事。相当于中文的 "请不要……"。

column1: If you add "-지 마세요" after a verb, it means the same as "Don't + verb" in English.
column2: 在动词后加 "-지 마세요"，意思和中文的 "别 + 动词" 一样。

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-지 마세요". It is the same with or without a final consonant.
column2: 去掉动词的 "-다"，加上 "-지 마세요"。有没有韵尾都一样。

column1: In English, "don't" comes before the verb, but in Korean "-지 마세요" comes after the verb.
column2: 中文的 "别/不要" 放在动词前面，而韩语的 "-지 마세요" 放在动词后面。

column1: 안 가세요? is not a command but a question (Aren't you going?). Don't use "안" to tell someone not to do something.
column2: 안 가세요? 不是禁止，而是问句 (您不去吗？)。叫别人不要做某事时不用 "안"。

column1: The form changes with the level of politeness. With friends or younger people, or in an emergency, use "-지 마" (만지지 마!); usually use "-지 마세요"; on signs and in announcements use "-지 마십시오".
column2: 形式随礼貌程度而变化。对朋友或晚辈，或在紧急情况下用 "-지 마" (만지지 마! 别碰！)；一般用 "-지 마세요"；标志和广播用 "-지 마십시오"。

column1: Don't run. The floor is slippery.
Can I turn on this coffee machine now?
column2: 这台咖啡机现在可以开吗？

column1: No, don't turn it on yet. It's being repaired.
OK, I understand. Then what shall I do?
column2: 好的，明白了。那我做什么？

column1: Move that box. It's heavy, so don't lift it alone.
column2: 把那个箱子搬走吧。很重，别一个人搬。

column1: Says what you must not do or what is not allowed. It is like "must not…, can't…" in English.
column2: 表示不能做的事或不被允许的事。相当于中文的 "不能……，不可以……"。

column1: After a final consonant (받침) add "-으면 안 돼요"; with no 받침 or with ㄹ 받침 add "-면 안 돼요".
column2: 有韵尾 (받침) 加 "-으면 안 돼요"；没有韵尾或韵尾是 ㄹ 时加 "-면 안 돼요"。

column1: -지 마세요 is said directly to the listener; "-(으)면 안 돼요" explains a rule.
column2: -지 마세요 是直接对听话人说的；"-(으)면 안 돼요" 是说明规则。

column1: As a question, "-(으)면 안 돼요?" asks for permission, like "Can't I…?": "조금 쉬면 안 돼요?" (Can't I rest a little?)
column2: 作为问句，"-(으)면 안 돼요?" 是请求许可，相当于 "不可以……吗？"："조금 쉬면 안 돼요?" (我不能休息一会儿吗？)
反义的说法是 "-아/어도 돼요" (可以)。

column1: You must not look at your phone during class.
You must not go in without permission.
Boss, can I listen to music while I work?
column2: 老板，我工作的时候可以听音乐吗？

column1: No, you must not wear earphones. You can't hear the customers.
column2: 不行，不能戴耳机。会听不见客人说话。

column1: to put on, wear (gloves, a ring)
Then what about during break time?
Shows permission: you may do it. As a question, it asks for permission. It is like "may…, can…, Can I…?" in English.
column2: 表示许可：可以做。作为问句，是请求许可。相当于中文的 "可以……，……可以吗？"。

column1: -아/어도 돼요 means "may…", and "-아/어도 돼요?" means "May I…?".
column2: -아/어도 돼요 意思是 "可以……"，"-아/어도 돼요?" 意思是 "我可以……吗？"。

column1: Take "요" off the "-아요/어요" form and add "-도 돼요".
column2: 去掉 "-아요/어요" 形式中的 "요"，加上 "-도 돼요"。

column1: In English "Can I…?" comes at the start, but Korean "-아/어도 돼요?" comes at the end: "Can I go first?" = "먼저 가도 돼요?"
column2: 中文的 "可以" 放在动词前面，而韩语的 "-아/어도 돼요?" 放在句末："我可以先走吗？" = "먼저 가도 돼요?"

column1: The answer is "네, 돼요" or "네, 그러세요"; if not allowed, "아니요, 안 돼요" or "-(으)면 안 돼요".
column2: 回答是 "네, 돼요" 或 "네, 그러세요"；不行时说 "아니요, 안 돼요" 或 "-(으)면 안 돼요"。

column1: -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요? asks if you are able to; "-아/어도 돼요?" asks for permission.
column2: -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요? 问的是有没有能力做；"-아/어도 돼요?" 是请求许可。

column1: May I go to the restroom?
Boss, may I go home a little early today?
column2: 老板，我今天可以早点走吗？

column1: Because I have to go to the bank.
Yes, you may go at five o'clock.
Says what you must do. It is like "must, have to" in English.
column2: 表示必须做的事。相当于中文的 "必须，得"。

column1: Take "요" off the "-아요/어요" form and add "-야 해요" or "-야 돼요". Both mean the same.
column2: 去掉 "-아요/어요" 形式中的 "요"，加上 "-야 해요" 或 "-야 돼요"。两者意思相同。

column1: English "have to" comes before the verb, but in Korean it is added after the verb: "have to go" = "가야 해요".
column2: 中文的 "得/必须" 放在动词前面，而韩语是加在动词后面："得去" = "가야 해요"。

column1: In speaking, "-야 돼요" is used a lot; in writing and formal speech, "-야 합니다" is common.
column2: 口语中常用 "-야 돼요"；书面语和正式场合常用 "-야 합니다"。

column1: Don't have to is "안 -아/어도 돼요", not "-지 않아야 해요".
column2: 不必 是 "안 -아/어도 돼요"，而不是 "-지 않아야 해요"。

column1: I have to hand in the assignment by tomorrow.
column2: 我得在明天之前交作业。

column1: I have to get up early tomorrow.
You have to take the medicine three times a day.
You must carry your residence card with you.
column2: 必须随身携带外国人登录证。

column1: I have to put them on
Sam, when you do the practice class, you must wear an apron.
column2: 山姆，上实习课时一定要穿围裙。

column1: Do I have to wear a hat too?
Yes, we are making food, so you have to wear a hat too.
column2: 是的，因为要做食物，所以帽子也得戴。

column1: Means doing just that is enough. Used when explaining how to do something. It is like "you just need to…, all you have to do is…" in English.
column2: 表示只要做这一点就够了。用于说明怎么做某事。相当于中文的 "只要……就行"。

column1: After a 받침 add "-으면 돼요"; with no 받침 or with ㄹ 받침 add "-면 돼요".
column2: 有韵尾加 "-으면 돼요"；没有韵尾或韵尾是 ㄹ 时加 "-면 돼요"。

column1: To ask how to do something, say "어떻게 하면 돼요?" (What should I do? / How do I do it?). It is the most useful question when learning a job.
column2: 问怎么做时说 "어떻게 하면 돼요?" (我该怎么做？)。这是学工作时最有用的问题。

column1: -아/어야 돼요 is something you must do; "-(으)면 돼요" means doing only that is enough.
column2: -아/어야 돼요 是必须做的事；"-(으)면 돼요" 表示只做这件事就足够了。

column1: You just need to press this button.
You only need to write your name here.
column2: 只要在这里写上名字就可以了。

column1: By what time should I come?
You just need to press it
You just need to put it in
You just need to do it
How do I use this washing machine?
First tap your student ID card, then just press the start button.
column2: 先刷学生证，然后按开始按钮就行。

column1: And when I want to stop it?
It is used in two ways: ① "-도록 하세요" is a polite instruction. ② "-도록" means "so that…, so as not to…".
column2: 有两种用法：① "-도록 하세요" 是礼貌的指示。② "-도록" 意思是 "为了……，以免……"。

column1: -도록 하세요 is a polite instruction, and "-지 않도록" means "so as not to…".
column2: -도록 하세요 是礼貌的指示，"-지 않도록" 意思是 "以免……"。

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-도록". It does not depend on 받침. For "so as not to", use "-지 않도록".
column2: 去掉动词的 "-다"，加上 "-도록"。和有没有韵尾无关。"以免" 用 "-지 않도록"。

column1: Seniors often use it when telling juniors what to do. The answer is "네, 그렇게 하겠습니다" or "-도록 하겠습니다".
column2: 上级对下级吩咐事情时常用。回答是 "네, 그렇게 하겠습니다" 或 "-도록 하겠습니다"。

column1: In school notices and dorm rules you often see "-지 않도록 주의하십시오": "물건을 잃어버리지 않도록 주의하십시오." (Be careful not to lose your things.)
column2: 学校通知或宿舍规则中常看到 "-지 않도록 주의하십시오"："물건을 잃어버리지 않도록 주의하십시오." (请注意不要丢失物品。)

column1: Be careful not to get hurt.
Tomorrow, please come by eight o'clock.
I left early so as not to be late.
column2: 为了不迟到，我早早出发了。

column1: I will be careful from now on.
Please make sure to do it
so as not to get hurt
so as not to be late
I will make sure to do it
Sam, you were late again today.
I'm sorry. I will make sure not to be late again.
column2: 对不起。我保证不会再迟到了。

column1: From the next class, please come ten minutes early.
column2: 从下节课开始，请提前十分钟到。

column1: Joins two sentences with "and". Used to list two similar actions or qualities side by side.
column2: 用 "而且，并且" 连接两个句子。用于并列两个相似的动作或性质。
-고 用 "而且，并且" 来连接句子。

column1: Take "-다" off a verb or adjective and add "-고". It does not depend on 받침. For nouns, use "(이)고".
column2: 去掉动词或形容词的 "-다"，加上 "-고"。和有没有韵尾无关。名词用 "(이)고"。

column1: Join a noun and a noun with "하고", and a sentence and a sentence with "-고": "밥하고 김치", "싸고 맛있어요".
column2: 名词和名词用 "하고" 连接，句子和句子用 "-고" 连接："밥하고 김치" (米饭和泡菜)，"싸고 맛있어요" (又便宜又好吃)。

column1: For the past, keep the first part as it is and change only the end: "싸고 맛있었어요."
column2: 过去的事也是前面不变，只改变句末："싸고 맛있었어요." (又便宜又好吃。)

column1: To split it into two sentences, use "그리고": "싸요. 그리고 맛있어요."
column2: 要分成两个句子时用 "그리고"："싸요. 그리고 맛있어요." (便宜。而且好吃。)

column1: This restaurant is cheap and tasty.
column2: 这家餐厅又便宜又好吃。

column1: The room is big and clean.
I study business administration, and my younger sibling works.
column2: 我学经营学，我弟弟/妹妹在工作。

column1: Sam is American, and Minha is Korean.
column2: 山姆是美国人，敏夏是韩国人。

column1: The room is spacious and clean.
Is it close to the school?
Means you finish the first action and then do the next one. It is like "…and then…, after…ing" in English.
column2: 表示做完前一个动作后再做下一个。相当于中文的 "……然后……，……之后"。

column1: -고 and "-고 나서" show the order of actions.
column2: -고 和 "-고 나서" 表示动作的先后顺序。

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-고" or "-고 나서". "-고 나서" makes it clearer that the first action is fully finished.
column2: 去掉动词的 "-다"，加上 "-고" 或 "-고 나서"。"-고 나서" 更明确地表示前一个动作已经完全结束。

column1: It is used very often when explaining steps: "신청서를 쓰고, 사진을 붙이고, 학과 사무실에 냅니다." (Write the application, attach a photo, and hand it in at the department office.)
column2: 说明步骤时非常常用："신청서를 쓰고, 사진을 붙이고, 학과 사무실에 냅니다." (填好申请表，贴上照片，交到系办公室。)

column1: Verbs of wearing and riding use "-고": "모자를 쓰고 나가요" (put on a hat and go out), "버스를 타고 가요" (go by bus).
column2: 表示穿戴和乘坐的动词用 "-고"："모자를 쓰고 나가요" (戴上帽子出门)，"버스를 타고 가요" (坐公交车去)。

column1: After "가다, 오다, 일어나다, 앉다, 만나다", use "-아서/어서", not "-고". You will learn this in the next set.
column2: 在 "가다、오다、일어나다、앉다、만나다" 后面不用 "-고"，而用 "-아서/어서"。这会在下一组学习。

column1: I finish my assignment and then rest.
Turn off the computer and then go out.
What did you do after dinner?
column2: 吃完晚饭后你做了什么？

column1: What do you do when work is finished?
I turn off the coffee machine and then wipe the tables.
column2: 我关掉咖啡机，然后擦桌子。

column1: I put away the cups and then go to the dorm.
column2: 我把杯子收拾好，然后回宿舍。

column1: to tidy up, to put away
Used when the first action and the next action are linked. You do the next action in the place of the first action, or in that state.
column2: 用于前后两个动作相互关联的时候。在做前一个动作的地方，或保持那个状态，做后一个动作。

column1: -아서/어서 tells two linked actions in order.
column2: -아서/어서 按顺序叙述两个相关联的动作。

column1: Take "요" off the "-아요/어요" form and add "서": 가다 → 가서, 만나다 → 만나서, 만들다 → 만들어서.
column2: 去掉 "-아요/어요" 形式中的 "요"，加上 "서"：가다 → 가서，만나다 → 만나서，만들다 → 만들어서。

column1: 시장에 가서 샀어요 means you bought it at the market. If you say "시장에 가고 샀어요", it sounds like two separate actions.
column2: 시장에 가서 샀어요 表示在市场买的。如果说 "시장에 가고 샀어요"，听起来像是两个分开的动作。

column1: Even for the past, do not add "-았/었-". "갔어서" is wrong; "가서" is right.
column2: 即使是过去的事，也不加 "-았/었-"。"갔어서" 是错的，"가서" 才对。

column1: I went to the market and bought apples.
I bought gimbap and ate it in the park.
column2: 我买了紫菜包饭，在公园吃了。

column1: I went to Seoul and met a friend.
What did you do after you met?
We went to a Nepali restaurant and ate.
column2: 我们去尼泊尔餐厅吃了饭。

column1: Means "before doing…". It is like "before" in English.
column2: 意思是 "做……之前"。相当于中文的 "……之前"。
动词 + -기 전에 意思是 "动词 + 之前"。

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-기 전에". For nouns, use "noun + 전에".
column2: 去掉动词的 "-다"，加上 "-기 전에"。名词用 "名词 + 전에"。

column1: The order is the opposite of English "before + verb": "before eating" = "먹기 전에".
column2: 语序和中文一样："吃饭之前" = "먹기 전에"。

column1: Even for the past, do not change the part before "-기 전에". "왔기 전에" is wrong.
column2: 即使是过去的事，"-기 전에" 前面也不变。"왔기 전에" 是错的。

column1: With time, use "time + 전에": "한 시간 전에" (an hour ago), "이 년 전에" (two years ago).
column2: 表示时间时用 "时间 + 전에"："한 시간 전에" (一小时前)，"이 년 전에" (两年前)。

column1: I wash my hands before eating.
Turn off your phone before class starts.
I learned Korean before I came to Korea.
column2: 来韩国之前我学过韩语。

column1: What do you have to do before the exam starts?
We have to put our student ID card on the desk.
column2: 要把学生证放在桌子上。

column1: Right. And before the exam ends?
We have to check our names again.
Means "after doing…". It is like "after" in English.
column2: 意思是 "做……之后"。相当于中文的 "……以后"。
动词 + -(으)ㄴ 후에 意思是 "动词 + 以后"。

column1: After a 받침 add "-은 후에"; with no 받침 add "-ㄴ 후에". "-(으)ㄴ 다음에" and "-(으)ㄴ 뒤에" mean the same. For nouns, use "noun + 후에".
column2: 有韵尾加 "-은 후에"；没有韵尾加 "-ㄴ 후에"。"-(으)ㄴ 다음에" 和 "-(으)ㄴ 뒤에" 意思相同。名词用 "名词 + 후에"。

column1: The order is the opposite of English "after + verb": "after eating" = "먹은 후에".
column2: 语序和中文一样："吃完以后" = "먹은 후에"。

column1: With time, use "time + 후에": "삼십 분 후에 오세요." (Please come in 30 minutes.)
column2: 表示时间时用 "时间 + 후에"："삼십 분 후에 오세요." (请30分钟后来。)

column1: On a medicine bag, "식후 30분" means "30 minutes after eating".
column2: 药袋上的 "식후 30분" 意思是 "饭后30分钟"。

column1: Let's meet after class is over.
Take the medicine after you eat.
After I came to Korea, I made many Korean friends.
column2: 来韩国后，我交了很多韩国朋友。

column1: What do you do after class?
When do I take this medicine?
Take it after meals. It's three times a day.
Do I take it right after eating?
Means doing two things at the same time. It is like "while …ing" in English.
column2: 表示同时做两件事。相当于中文的 "一边……一边……"。

column1: -(으)면서 means one person does two things at the same time.
column2: -(으)면서 表示一个人同时做两件事。

column1: After a 받침 add "-으면서"; with no 받침 or with ㄹ 받침 add "-면서".
column2: 有韵尾加 "-으면서"；没有韵尾或韵尾是 ㄹ 时加 "-면서"。

column1: The same person must do both actions. If the people are different, use "-는 동안".
column2: 做两件事的必须是同一个人。如果是不同的人，要用 "-는 동안"。

column1: Say the more important action last: "운전하면서 전화하지 마세요." (Don't talk on the phone while driving.)
column2: 把更重要的动作放在后面说："운전하면서 전화하지 마세요." (开车时不要打电话。)

column1: 듣다 becomes "들으면서" and 걷다 becomes "걸으면서" (ㄷ irregular).
column2: 듣다 变成 "들으면서"，걷다 变成 "걸으면서" (ㄷ 不规则)。

column1: I study while listening to music.
column2: 我一边听音乐一边学习。
我们一边吃饭一边聊天。

column1: I learned Korean while working part-time.
column2: 我一边打工一边学了韩语。

column1: Looking at your phone while walking is dangerous.
column2: 边走路边看手机很危险。
我一边看电视剧一边学的。

column1: Isn't it hard to study while working?
column2: 一边工作一边学习不累吗？

column1: Means during the time something is going on. It is like "while, during" in English.
column2: 表示在某事进行的期间。相当于中文的 "在……的时候，……期间"。

column1: -는 동안 means "while…", and "time + 동안" means "for (a time)".
column2: -는 동안 意思是 "在……的时候"，"时间 + 동안" 意思是 "(一段时间) 期间"。

column1: Take "-다" off the verb and add "-는 동안". A ㄹ 받침 drops (돌다 → 도는 동안). For nouns, use "noun + 동안".
column2: 去掉动词的 "-다"，加上 "-는 동안"。韵尾 ㄹ 会脱落 (돌다 → 도는 동안)。名词用 "名词 + 동안"。

column1: The subjects of the two parts can be different: "제가 청소하는 동안 아이샤 씨가 요리했어요." (While I cleaned, Aisha cooked.)
column2: 前后的主语可以不同："제가 청소하는 동안 아이샤 씨가 요리했어요." (我打扫的时候，爱莎做了饭。)

column1: To say how long something took, use "time + 동안": "얼마 동안 한국에 있었어요?" (How long were you in Korea?)
column2: 说花了多长时间时用 "时间 + 동안"："얼마 동안 한국에 있었어요?" (你在韩国待了多久？)

column1: It often appears in exam rules: "시험을 보는 동안 휴대폰을 끄십시오." (Turn off your phone while taking the exam.)
column2: 常出现在考试规则中："시험을 보는 동안 휴대폰을 끄십시오." (考试期间请关闭手机。)

column1: Please be quiet while my roommate is sleeping.
